value.text: An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his K9 partner joined a search effort to locate a missing 84-year-old woman with dementia while attending a K9 certification course in Gadsden County near Tallahassee. Body camera footage from Deputy Sam Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area to assist in the search. Bloodhound search teams from across the state, including Indian River County, participated in the effort. "They had a rotated dog search, so Penny searched and some of the other dogs searched as well," Lt. Margaret Myles Ellis was reported missing on Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before. Officials said Ellis had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Ellis was found approximately 30 hours later in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety. They're coming out," the body camera footage captured. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Jaworski said. He expressed pride in the entire K9 unit, which includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. "Luckily, they were at the right place at the right time. We're extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and our entire K9 unit that, you know, goes out every day," Jaworski said. Jaworski also highlighted the unique role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies. "Dogs don't judge you, you know they love everybody, so it's a good way to connect and it opens up the door to express some of these things that we see and hear every day," he said. Ellis was reunited with her family, and Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned home and resumed their duties. Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. WPTV is learning more details about what led up to a shooting at a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie last weekend.According to the incident report, the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space. Multiple witnesses provided accounts of the incident to responding officers.One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.Another witness who came to pick up an Uber order said she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. She said the man was staring while he walked to the door, and when she looked away and got out of her vehicle to pick up the order, the man began yelling. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and continued to lunge. The witness said the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to "come outside." The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris "ran up on him with a knife."Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene.The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed with WPTV that Harris, despite being the victim of the incident, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Florida Panthers preseason is underway, and one of the biggest storylines is new acquisition Brady Tkachuk — a star in his own right and the younger brother of Panthers forward Matthew Tkachuk.Brady, the former captain of the Ottawa Senators, sat down with WPTV anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim to talk about joining South Florida's roster.WATCH: Brady Tkachuk joins Panthers, says family bond with brother Matthew makes South Florida specialWhen asked how it feels to be in South Florida, Brady kept it simple."It's pretty special. It's been awesome down here so far," Brady said.Beyond hockey, Brady said the opportunity to raise his family near his brother's is something he does not take lightly."You know, our families, it's just, you know, our kids growing up together and, uh, you know, for my kids seeing, um, you know, Matthew and Ellie a lot and then the same thing for, for Millie seeing us that just gonna be so special that you know we're not going to take a second for granted," Brady said.General manager Bill Zito has expressed confidence that Brady will fit seamlessly into the Panthers' lineup. Brady appears to share that outlook, pointing to the team's depth as a strength."Yeah, I mean, I think for, for me it's the only thing that, that matters is the 2 points for our team and, and I think that. Everybody in that room can be saying the same thing. So, um, on any given night we have such a deep, great team that a guy can step up and produce," Brady said.Coming in as a former captain and offensive focal point, Brady was asked whether putting up personal points remains a priority. His answer pointed squarely to the team.As for comparisons to his older brother Matthew — widely regarded as one of the game's elite players — Brady deflected any suggestion that he has the edge."He's, he's the biggest motivator. Just see how great that he is that, you know, if I'm to be half the player that he is, I'd be, I'd be very lucky," Brady said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Coco Gauff will be a player-owner for the Florida franchise that will compete in the new season of World Team Tennis.The two-time Grand Slam singles champion is scheduled to play in the Florida Flamingos Racquet Club's home matches on Dec. The team will play in Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, home of the NHL's Florida Panthers.Gauff grew up in Delray Beach, Florida."I'm looking forward to playing at home in front of my family and friends in South Florida," Gauff said Thursday in a statement. "It’s not often, as a tennis player, that we get to compete as part of a team, so I’m excited for the new experience, not only for myself but, even more importantly, for the fans."The Flamingos were one of the original franchises when World Team Tennis began in 1974 as a way of having a mixed-gender team format for tennis, with Hall of Famer Billie Jean King among the founders.It returns in December with the other teams based in New York and Toronto. Open semifinalists Frances Tiafoe and Jessica Pegula will be teammates for New York Empire Racquet Club, while the Toronto North Racquet Club features Canadian players Denis Shapovalov, Leylah Fernandez, Victoria Mboko and Gabriel Diallo.Gauff's teammates include Tommy Paul, Learner Tien, Iva Jovic, Brandon Nakashima and Eva Lys.The league will have a new match format featuring four singles sets (a men’s and women’s No. 2), and a mixed doubles super tiebreaker. Each team will start two men and two women.

A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. By: Mike Trim Posted LAKE WORTH, Fla — A nonprofit based in Palm Beach County that sends care packages to our military men and women stationed around the world is asking for your help. Forgotten Soldiers Outreach tells me it's running critically low on donated supplies. WATCH BELOW: Nonprofit running low on supplies for military care packages They send monthly care packages to more than 5,200 active duty military units. I connected with the organization's leadership at its headquarters in Lake Worth earlier this year and have even brought my own family to prepare the packages. The executive director tells me that extended deployments due to the war in Iran and new units requesting packages are dwindling their supplies. A detailed list of needed items is available on the Forgotten Soldiers Outreach website .

By: Samantha Roesler Posted and last updated STUART, Fla. — A semi tractor-trailer fire has forced a closure of a major roadway in Stuart, affecting traffic flow and school access Wednesday morning. SW Pratt Whitney Road is completely closed from just south of SW Bulldog Way to Bridge Road as emergency crews respond to the incident. The closure is impacting access to South Fork High School, with only students and staff able to reach the campus from the northern approach. No injuries have been reported at this time, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation. Motorists are urged to avoid the area entirely and seek alternate routes. The closure is expected to remain in effect until the scene is cleared and the roadway is deemed safe for travel.

A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced on Tuesday, Sept. 22, that it arrested a 15-year-old Martin County High School student in connection with a false bomb threat made against the school. The sheriff’s office said its school resource officers and criminal investigations division traced the originator of the message back to the 15-year-old student, who is a sophomore at the school. WPBF 25 News is not publishing the name of the suspect because the student is under the age of 18 and has not been charged as an adult. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The sheriff’s office said the student confessed to sending the hoax threat. The student is facing a charge of false report concerning the planting of a bomb, which is a second-degree felony. “This arrest follows multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in our area over the past several weeks. Each threat is taken seriously and requires a significant response from law enforcement and emergency personnel, regardless of whether the threat ultimately proves to be a hoax,” the sheriff’s office said. It added that the suspect was only linked to the threat to the high school on Tuesday, Sept. “The Sheriff’s Office will thoroughly investigate these incidents and aggressively pursue those responsible when the investigation provides sufficient evidence to identify them. To anyone who thinks sending a threat anonymously, by text, online or through another form of electronic communication will automatically protect you from being identified and charged: that is not a safe assumption. These are not jokes, and will be treated as the crimes that they are.” Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

A tax break for Florida homeowners could bring a bigger bill for renters next door, according to a new report examining Amendment 3.The report released by the Florida Housing Coalition estimates that if local governments raise property-tax rates to replace revenue lost under the amendment, annual taxes would increase by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028.Watch more from Forrest Saunders on the reportJared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report, said much of that expense could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents.“Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check,” Walczak said.Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences. School district property taxes would remain unchanged.Rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption.Local governments facing lost revenue could respond by cutting spending, increasing property-tax rates, raising other taxes or fees, or combining those approaches. Walczak’s analysis models rate increases intended to replace lost revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates.“While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent,” he said.The estimates represent average increases in property-tax bills. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions.By 2031, the report estimates the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach.The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties: It would lower the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. That limits assessment growth, while allowing local tax rates to rise. Walczak's report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift.Supporters, including Florida Realtors, argue that homeowners also need help with housing costs.“Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayer," said Margy Grant of Florida Realtors.The potential loss of local revenue has also drawn opposition from the Florida Sheriffs Association, which warns the amendment could squeeze funding for deputies and other public-safety needs.Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz pushed back against those warnings in a statement posted on X.“Tax relief and public safety are not competing priorities,” she said.Cordero-Stutz urged government agencies, including sheriffs’ offices, to examine their spending and eliminate unnecessary costs while protecting essential law-enforcement resources.Gov. Ron DeSantis supports Amendment 3 and says future lawmakers will pursue targeted state grants to help maintain essential services. He said the Legislature did not include the grant fund he sought in the amendment and that he plans to work with lawmakers on assistance."We will ensure that essential services continue, but we also recognize taxpayers need a break" DeSantis said.Florida voters will decide the measure Nov. The proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% of the votes cast on it to pass.

Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

Drought Monitor update shows improvement across portions of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, although dry conditions have not disappeared entirely especially farther inland. The map, released Thursday and based on conditions through Tuesday morning, compares the latest drought picture with last week’s update. It does not measure rainfall alone. The weekly analysis also considers soil moisture, streamflow, groundwater and longer-term precipitation trends, so improvement after a wet stretch can take time to show up. Palm Beach County sees the clearest improvement The most noticeable change is across much of eastern and central Palm Beach County. Areas that were classified in moderate drought last week are now shown as abnormally dry in the latest update. That is a step in the right direction, but it does not mean the area is completely free of dryness. Moderate drought continues across parts of western Palm Beach County, including areas closer to the Lake Okeechobee agricultural region. Those locations will need more sustained rainfall to see additional improvement. Okeechobee County remains a mixed picture Okeechobee County also shows some improvement, with more of the county now classified as abnormally dry rather than moderate drought. However, a pocket of severe drought remains in the southwestern part of the county. That means water resources and agricultural interests there remain especially sensitive to an extended dry period. Treasure Coast conditions hold steady to improve slightly Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties continue to show a mix of abnormally dry conditions and areas that are not in drought. The latest map keeps much of the remaining dryness focused away from the immediate coast, while coastal sections have either held steady or seen modest improvement from last week. For residents, abnormally dry is the lowest level on the Drought Monitor scale and is not the same as an official drought designation. Still, it is a signal that rainfall and water conditions are running below where they should be. Moderate and severe drought categories indicate a greater and more persistent moisture deficit. The recent run of showers and thunderstorms has helped, and the changing weather pattern may bring additional opportunities for rain before drier air becomes more established. Even so, the update shows that one wet week does not erase a longer-term rainfall shortfall overnight. The main takeaway: drought conditions are trending in a better direction for parts of the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, particularly east of Lake Okeechobee, but inland areas will need more consistent rainfall to keep that improvement going.

A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

Three earlier threats still under investigation: The Sheriff’s Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. For families such as Maya and Liz, the concern now is whether the threats will stop. The advice I give to my daughter is to stay calm. She’s very smart and quick to think, and I tell her to do what God is telling her right away. Follow the rules and what the teachers tell you, but you have to react how you feel in that moment. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Martin County High School released the following statement: The safety and security of our students and staff remains our top priority. We appreciate the swift response and coordination of the Martin County Sheriff's Office, our School Resource Officers, and the District's Safety and Security Team, whose efforts allowed yesterday's false FortifyFL report involving Martin County High School to be quickly investigated, determined to be unfounded, and ultimately resolved with an arrest. Because the report was confirmed to be false, there is no additional law enforcement presence on campus related to this incident. Our two School Resource Officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of our normal daily safety operations. We also want to be clear: false threats and false reports are not pranks. They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. Individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable, exactly as how it unfolded yesterday. We understand these threats can cause fear and distress, and when we talk about student safety, we want them to feel safe as well. We will be providing additional services and staff during the school day, including School Social Service Workers and School Counselors, and we encourage students who need support to talk with them. We continue to encourage students, staff, and families to report legitimate safety concerns. Every report is taken seriously and investigated thoroughly because protecting our students and staff will always come first.

A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. A man with decades of experience in cybersecurity found a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven , and police are now investigating. Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose. "I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said. Bess said skimmers take almost no time to put on. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. Bess said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating. Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. See also: Is it illegal to drive with hazard lights on in the rain? It depends; here's the law The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all. "My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen. We'll have an update on the investigation from the Fort Pierce Police Department, and we'll give you the details when they become available.

With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

A Delray Beach family is demanding accountability from the city after discovering that a burial plot they had purchased years ago at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery was sold and used to bury someone else.The discovery has caused significant heartbreak for Delila Kellum and her family, who were unable to fulfill her father's final wish to be buried next to his brother."It's just heartbreak; it's upsetting," Kellum told WPTV. "We can't bury him where he wanted, so we haven’t really decided what to do."WPTV's Zitlali Solache has been covering multiple concerns involving the cemetery's overcapacity, maintenance, and record-keeping, pressing the city for answers. WATCH: Family seeks answers after pre-purchased burial plot was sold to someone elseThe issue began in 2010 when Kellum and her sister took their father to visit his late brother's grave. Their parents had purchased two adjacent plots."When we took him to there, we got out and looked at the stone and when we look over... we noticed somebody was buried in my mother’s spot," Kellum said.The family immediately contacted the city but were told the body could not be moved. According to Kellum, a supervisor offered them two different plots and promised to provide new deeds."To this day we've never seen them," Kellum said. "My sister tried to contact them when my father passed, but nothing."When her father died in 2024, the family was faced with a devastating reality. "We couldn't put him in his spot next to his brother, we had to get him cremated," she explained, adding they skipped a proper funeral.Kellum said her mother suffers from dementia and is unaware of the distressing situation. "Now we’re just gonna wait for my mother to pass and have it together," she said.This is not the first time the Kellum family has encountered issues with the cemetery's record-keeping. Kellum said they have also struggled to locate the grave of her grandfather, a Pearl Harbor veteran.Although the city initially denied he was buried there, Kellum stated that funeral home officials provided documents proving his interment at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery."We went to go try to find him and we couldn't find him," she said.The family has documents, including a deed from 1994, which they believe prove their ownership of the original plots.The Kellum family's experience is part of a larger pattern of concerns WPTV has been following regarding burial records, capacity and maintenance at the city-run cemetery.In response to these issues, the city of Delray Beach has hired Kuehne Cemetery Consulting to conduct an independent assessment of the cemetery's operations.According to a statement from the city, the review will cover administration, record-keeping, maintenance, customer service, and financial sustainability. The firm will provide a report with prioritized recommendations for immediate and long-term improvements.A community meeting to discuss the cemetery is scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 30.For Kellum, the actions are long overdue. She wants the city to be held responsible for the distress her family has endured."They should be held accountable for what they've done all these years," she said. "I'd just like to put my parents where they're supposed to be."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County.The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95.WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearanceAt around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard.Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118.During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. Some residents in Port St. Lucie and their homeowners' association are at odds over dead trees. People who live in Cadence at Tradition received a notice dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc., saying the dead tree or dead trees on their property need to be replaced. The notice says: "Your assistance and cooperation are requested regarding the following: Landscaping-Dead Tree- The deceased tree(s) on your property is in need of attention." Residents say the trees are on the swale, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and numerous trees were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the swale, some residents say it should be the HOA 's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners. "It's just a little bit frustrating and disappointing that we, as homeowners, have to endure this from the HOA," said Keyla Peguero, a homeowner at Cadence at Tradition. Recently the HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees, at the homeowners' expense. But homeowners such as Chip Collison say the dead trees were in common areas, not their yards, so they want the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. "You think the swale is a common area?" we asked Collison. "Based on the documentation I've read? The notice sent to homeowners goes on to say: "We kindly request you address this matter by 9/30/26 to avoid escalation." See also: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees. Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead. "We're well into hurricane season now. If we plant new trees, no one can predict the future. These trees could be freshly planted. We get a strong hurricane come through, they're all gone, and they're gonna have to be redone again," Collison said. Peguero says she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house, at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it with a new tree. She says she's not willing to do it again and shouldn't have had to do it in the first place. A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA sent us this written statement: Currently, the HOA is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in the common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. In the limited common areas, such as the rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons, residents are responsible for replacing trees and maintaining these areas. Because the HOA is currently purchasing and installing trees in bulk, we’ve invited residents to participate in the program. This allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring that tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally.

A confrontation at a school bus stop in Indiantown, where a father pulled a gun on two teenagers after his son reported being bullied, has sparked community discussions and involvement from the NAACP. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said the incident began last Thursday when the man’s son reported being bullied. The next day, the father went to the bus stop to drop off his son and started speaking with the bus driver. According to the sheriff, two students then left the bus and confronted the father. “The dad's got his hand up, telling them to stay back, stay back, stay back,” said Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek. The sheriff explained that the father pulled out a concealed weapon when the teens approached him. “They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do. He's legally allowed to stand his ground,” Budensiek said. The two students involved, Trevor Ivory and RJ McIntyre, shared their perspective on the incident. “I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school,” Ivory said. “Instead, they had to see a man with a gun on two teenagers that they know ride the bus in the morning.” The confrontation was a key topic during an NAACP community meeting held Tuesday night. The two students and their families attended the meeting, where emotions ran high. “The dad had a thousand options. He chose the wrong option,” said Pam Ivory, Trevor’s aunt. Jimmy Smith, president of the NAACP Martin County Branch, also addressed the situation. “We know guns aren’t allowed on school property. They also shouldn’t be allowed in school bus stops,” Smith said. Smith added that he plans to meet with the school board and the sheriff to discuss the incident further. “We shouldn’t be pointing a gun at our children,” he said. The sheriff’s office stated that it conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had chosen to press charges. However, no arrests have been made, and the sheriff reiterated that the father acted within the law.
