At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he’s often tried to avoid. “Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff’s department, Indian River County,” reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. It’s the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. “I was 22,” Marc said quietly. “I was 22.” It’s always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that’s brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he’s come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he’s been longing to give. And it’s finally over,” Marc said. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida’s 18th this year. It is scheduled for October 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. “It gives closure,” Marc said. “Now, when everybody asks me, ‘What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?’ That the first question I get, and I got to say, ‘He’s still — still hasn’t happened.” “You’ll finally have a different answer,” Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey supplied. “Yes, finally have a different answer,” Marc replied. On September 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot 4 times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer. Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he “panicked” when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. “One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother’s friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn’t make it. I knew he didn’t make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that,” Marc told WFLX. “How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God’s sake’s. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?” In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother’s grave, waiting and wondering. “Wondering what’s happened. Feels like everybody forgot,” Marc said. Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. “It’s something I wouldn’t wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through,” Marc said. “No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn’t decorate.” When DeSantis signed Reaves’ death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted. It’s finally over,” Marc said. The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves’ death warrant to be signed. “All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it’s going to be a moment of healing for our agency,” Flowers told WFLX. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves’ execution. “Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform,” said Flowers. Reaves’ execution would mark Florida’s 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out. “One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don’t know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don’t know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved,” Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said. Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski’s family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. “And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family’s experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family’s pain was not going to give us closure or peace,” said Hanna. “Though certainly don’t hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure.” For Marc, standing at his brother’s grave — a place that will always hold pain — he’s reminded of all he’s lost. “The time I never got to spend with him,” Marc said, holding back tears. “Mom and Dad didn’t see any closure in this, time that they didn’t get to spend with him, time he didn’t get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It’s all very much to take in.” Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. “He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he’s the one that found him out in the woods by the facility,” Marc recalled. “He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around.” Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought. “There is finally closure for Richard,” Marc said. “For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there.” This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. More details are being released about a road rage incident in Port St. Lucie that escalated into a shooting Thursday evening, resulting in one man being injured and both drivers arrested on felony charges. Lucie police received a 911 call around 6:30 p.m. reporting gunshots in a residential neighborhood near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace. "Gunshots in front of my house," a caller said during the emergency call. The caller also described the aftermath of the shooting. "I heard it, and then I saw a guy raising his hands up and said he had blood on his hands," the caller said. Investigators said the altercation began as a misunderstanding during a lane change and merge near SW Crosstown Parkway. The situation escalated into a physical confrontation when 41-year-old Dean Plotts exited his vehicle, approached 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, who was seated in his car, and punched him through the window. "He stepped out of his vehicle, approached the other man who was seated inside his vehicle, and punched him inside his vehicle, so now he's breaking the plane of the window," the Port St. Lucie police chief Leo Niemczyk said. "Therefore, entering, which makes it a burglary of the conveyance with the intention of committing a crime, being battery by punching the other individual who is seated inside the vehicle." Plotts then returned to his vehicle, but the confrontation escalated further. "Almost makes it back to his vehicle and starts getting fire on," Niemczyk said. Police said Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Both men were arrested, with Plotts facing charges for initiating the physical altercation and Kukielka for firing his weapon. When asked if Kukielka’s actions could be considered self-defense, Niemczyk said, "It's not self-defense at that point. If Plotts had been coming at him at that point, the shooting may well have been justified, but it was actually just the reverse. He was fleeing from him." Both men are now facing felony charges. Because one thought the other one may have cut the other one off when they were both turning into the same roadway. Again, no reason to be facing felony charges; let it go, let it go," Niemczyk said. A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

"Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

A confrontation in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot ended with a man shot in the chest and later facing charges. 19, officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. for reports of a shooting. Officers found the suspect, Christopher Harris, suffering from a single gunshot wound to his chest. Police say Harris was armed with a knife and shot after starting an argument with another man over a parking space. Shoppers were surprised to hear about the violence at the busy shopping plaza, especially in the middle of the day. That's a horrible story to hear," said Sharon Osceola of Okeechobee. "It's a nice neighborhood. You don't ever see any confrontations happening in this area." The shooting led to a heavy law enforcement investigation outside the business , with crime scene tape around the restaurant. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm. Investigators say Davis shot Harris in self-defense. PSLPD said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris allegedly followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso, according to PSLPD. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor, according to PSLPD. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. "Being here for so long, you just never had a lot of crime here," said Angel Vazquez of Port St. "It's shocking but it is getting a little crazy here in this city here." Police said Harris was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sunday after he was treated and released from the hospital.

Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. Lucie road rage incident that escalated into a physical fight and shooting landed two men in handcuffs Thursday. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Police said that before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following, police said. One of the drivers, identified as Tylon Kukielka, 57, was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as Dean Plotts, 41, was traveling in the same direction. Police said the situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace, when Plotts got out of his truck and confronted Kukielka's car. "He got out of his vehicle and approached the other vehicle, which was parked in front of him, and he approached it, and he punched the driver of that vehicle through the open window," said Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk. See also: Formerly conjoined twins see each other face-to-face after historic separation surgery Investigators say Plotts went back to his own vehicle, but Kukielka followed with a gun and shot him multiple times. While an arrest report indicates the two men were facing each other when the shots were fired, Niemczyk said Plotts wasn't confronting Kukielka again he was trying to get away. "The reason they were facing the same direction is because he was turning to his open car door, [trying] to get back in his vehicle," Niemczyk said. "So he wasn't actually going back to confront [him]." A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Detectives later charged Kukielka with attempted homicide. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery a charge Niemczyk said surprises people unfamiliar with the statute. "Most people will associate that with a house or a business," Niemczyk said. "But you can also commit burglary of a conveyance, which is a vehicle. So by punching the individual, he broke the plane of that vehicle." The incident remains under investigation. Niemczyk said road rage incidents like this one have become more common in Port St. "I would say over the last few years, yeah, we've had quite a few road rage incidents in this city," Niemczyk said. "And obviously with the increased volume of traffic in the community and the congestion that a lot of our residents are accustomed to, frustration comes along with that."

A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. Before an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City , a man allegedly threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend after she went to his home to check on him following their breakup, a new report reveals. According to an arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the ex-girlfriend of the suspect, Darrel Abbey, arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts, according to the report. The woman told investigators Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated. The arrest report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman, "I should die, you should kill me," while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey continued yelling at the woman while recording the interaction on his phone. The woman told investigators that Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed, according to the report. Investigators said Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey allegedly continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. The report says that when Abbey picked up the gun again, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now." Investigators said Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. As Abbey walked outside, the woman told investigators she heard several loud "pop" sounds. Abbey then returned inside to retrieve a rifle and allegedly tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey allegedly told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it. At some point during the incident, Abbey allegedly began cleaning the firearms and said, "I gotta wipe all my fingerprints off, I gotta get the gunshot residue off of my hands, I'm not going back to prison." The report says Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink, prompting the woman to begin recording him. Investigators who reviewed the video said Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he allegedly reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her. Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Investigators also said Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

A 15-year-old student was arrested Tuesday after threatening Martin County High School , according to the district. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. The threat was reported on the FortifyFL portal around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. Investigators traced the report to a student identification number associated with Taylor. When questioned, Taylor acknowledged making the report but initially claimed the report came from other students. According to the affidavit, Taylor could not provide identifying information about the alleged students or describe their voices. The student also refused a request to search a personally owned Chromebook. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 Investigators then reviewed school surveillance footage and saw Taylor walking past a bathroom with another student. That student told investigators Taylor said a tip would be created anonymously and would not be traced back to Taylor, according to the affidavit. Taylor was advised of constitutional rights and agreed to speak with investigators. Taylor's laptop was then confiscated as evidence. The investigation resulted in probable cause to book the student for false report concerning planting a bomb, according to the affidavit. Taylor was taken into custody and transported to the Martin County Sheriff's Office jail before being transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. The original threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The district previously notified families that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said Taylor can only be linked to this specific threat. False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Principal Lori Vogel said, adding that false threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms or other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

A proposed luxury waterfront development in Fort Pierce is drawing renewed attention after city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring outside legal counsel to review whether the city has any options to challenge the project under Florida's Live Local Act. 14 vote comes as cities across Florida continue testing the limits of the state's Live Local Act and lawmakers implement the latest round of changes to the law. The proposed Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island has become one of the Treasure Coast's most closely watched growth disputes, putting residents and local officials at odds with a state law that limits how much control cities have over certain housing projects. 14 meeting, the commission approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether Fort Pierce has any legal grounds to challenge the project under the Live Local Act. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions. The move comes as Florida enters the latest phase of the law. Known as Live Local 4.0, the most recent changes took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing. Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would change the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he’s often tried to avoid. “Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff’s department, Indian River County,” reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. It’s the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. “I was 22,” Marc said quietly. “I was 22.” It’s always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that’s brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he’s come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he’s been longing to give. And it’s finally over,” Marc said. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida’s 18th this year. It is scheduled for October 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. “It gives closure,” Marc said. “Now, when everybody asks me, ‘What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?’ That the first question I get, and I got to say, ‘He’s still — still hasn’t happened.” “You’ll finally have a different answer,” Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey supplied. “Yes, finally have a different answer,” Marc replied. On September 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot 4 times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer. Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he “panicked” when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. “One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother’s friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn’t make it. I knew he didn’t make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that,” Marc told WFLX. “How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God’s sake’s. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?” In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother’s grave, waiting and wondering. “Wondering what’s happened. Feels like everybody forgot,” Marc said. Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. “It’s something I wouldn’t wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through,” Marc said. “No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn’t decorate.” When DeSantis signed Reaves’ death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted. It’s finally over,” Marc said. The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves’ death warrant to be signed. “All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it’s going to be a moment of healing for our agency,” Flowers told WFLX. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves’ execution. “Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform,” said Flowers. Reaves’ execution would mark Florida’s 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out. “One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don’t know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don’t know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved,” Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said. Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski’s family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. “And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family’s experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family’s pain was not going to give us closure or peace,” said Hanna. “Though certainly don’t hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure.” For Marc, standing at his brother’s grave — a place that will always hold pain — he’s reminded of all he’s lost. “The time I never got to spend with him,” Marc said, holding back tears. “Mom and Dad didn’t see any closure in this, time that they didn’t get to spend with him, time he didn’t get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It’s all very much to take in.” Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. “He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he’s the one that found him out in the woods by the facility,” Marc recalled. “He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around.” Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought. “There is finally closure for Richard,” Marc said. “For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there.” This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris’ waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris’ front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

With just weeks to go before voters decide the fate of Amendment 3, one of the most talked-about questions across Palm Beach County remains the same: What does it mean for my wallet?WPTV has been following the debate for months as county leaders, residents and taxpayers weigh the potential benefits and drawbacks of the controversial property tax proposal that will appear on the November ballot.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 calculator to launch in Palm Beach CountyNow, Palm Beach County homeowners have a new tool aimed at answering that question with personalized numbers."We're excited to launch the Amendment 3 calculator, which will let residents, homesteaded residents, actually look up their own property and find out what their taxes could be after Amendment 3 passes, should it pass," Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said.The new online Amendment 3 calculator allows homesteaded property owners to enter their address and see an estimate of how the proposed constitutional amendment could affect their property taxes, along with the potential revenue impact on local taxing authorities.The calculator goes live at 7 a.m. Wednesday on the Property Appraiser's website.Amendment 3 has become a regular topic at county meetings as officials discuss their budgets and what could happen if voters approve the measure.The amendment requires at least 60% voter approval on Nov. According to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's Office, the exemption could increase to as much as $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School taxes would not receive the same increase.Supporters argue it would provide much-needed tax relief for homeowners dealing with rising costs."I plan to vote to eliminate property taxes," said Gillian Lieberman, a Palm Beach County property owner and real estate professional. "People work hard, and I think everyone that I work with, my colleagues, my friends, my clients, they work hard, and I'd like them to see that money back in their pocket as much as possible."Lieberman said she believes property owners could use the savings."We have such a great city, great infrastructure, great development, and I don't think eliminating property taxes is going to hurt that. I think it's going to allow owners to do more and purchase more so they have less stress when the tax bill comes," she said.Others are concerned about the potential loss of funding for community services.Logan Mroczkowski, a Palm Beach County homeowner, pointed to local parks and public amenities that benefit from property tax revenue."I work in Lake Worth, and I spent a lot of time at Bryant Park. I spent a lot of time there on my lunch breaks for work, and I know that the property taxes pay for a significant amount of the upkeep, the maintenance, stuff like that," Mroczkowski said. "I'm a big fan of when taxes are utilized to better the community."While acknowledging the referendum could save him money personally, Mroczkowski said he currently plans to vote against it."I am personally of the opinion that I'm probably going to vote no on the referendum. I know it could save me money, but unselfishly, I think it's more important that those taxes are used to better the community," Mroczkowski said.Jacks said the potential impact stretches far beyond individual homeowners.According to Jacks, that equates to roughly "$324 million in tax revenue that would go away."She noted that's only the county's share."And that's just the county. There's certainly many other taxing authorities that would also see similar reductions," Jacks said.The new calculator is designed to help residents understand both sides of that equation."We also wanted people to understand the two sides to Amendment 3, the one side that yes, I, as a homesteader, would save more, but also there's an impact to the many taxing authorities that each of us pay and to sort of share with them what that impact would be when you start bundling together 300,000 homesteads in Palm Beach County, not just my own," Jacks said.Residents with a homestead exemption can simply enter their address to generate an estimate."You would just put your address into this field here and then of course it just goes down and gives you the data," Jacks explained.The calculator will show current estimated taxes, projected changes for 2027 and 2028 if Amendment 3 passes, and estimated revenue impacts to local taxing districts.Jacks said the system will also indicate if a property does not have a homestead exemption and therefore is not eligible for the proposed tax benefit.The projections are based on 2026 certified property values and millage rates.She cautioned that future tax bills could still vary."That depends on the millage rates, which can change. They could go up, and it also depends on their value, which also could go up," Jacks said.Because the calculator uses parcel-level data, Jacks believes it can offer a clearer picture than broad statewide estimates."I think because we're able to do it at the parcel level, so individually, it's probably one of the more accurate," Jacks said.The tool also accounts for local differences."Absolutely, that's the point," Jacks said when asked whether results will vary depending on where someone lives. It's what you're paying."Jacks emphasized that the Property Appraiser's Office is not advocating for or against the amendment."It's really here to educate and nothing more," Jacks said.Instead, she hopes the calculator gives residents a way to move beyond campaign rhetoric and evaluate the proposal based on their own situation."So often these amendments appear on the ballot, and there isn't really a tool or a resource you can go to to say OK, well, how is that going to affect me and we thought this would be a good way to do that," Jacks said.Ultimately, she said, the goal is simple."We're hoping that the public will say, wow, you know, OK, let me look at my numbers and let me make a decision based on my numbers as opposed to all this chatter going on," Jacks said.For Palm Beach County voters still deciding how they'll cast their ballot in November, that personalized look may arrive just in time.The Amendment 3 Homestead Calculator becomes available at 7 a.m. Wednesday on the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's website.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Spam calls and text messages are a frustration shared by millions of people, and one local man says the problem has gotten out of hand.Recently, I heard from Mark Shubert about the unwanted calls he was getting every day.WATCH BELOW: How you can reduce those annoying spam calls, texts "Really very infuriating; that's why I contacted you because I didn't know where to turn," Shubert said. Making the calls stop is not easy, but there are things we can do. "I was starting to just receive an alarming number of calls," says Kim Key, senior security writer at PC Mag. A 15-year-old student was arrested Tuesday after threatening Martin County High School , according to the district. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. The threat was reported on the FortifyFL portal around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. Investigators traced the report to a student identification number associated with Taylor. When questioned, Taylor acknowledged making the report but initially claimed the report came from other students. According to the affidavit, Taylor could not provide identifying information about the alleged students or describe their voices. The student also refused a request to search a personally owned Chromebook. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 Investigators then reviewed school surveillance footage and saw Taylor walking past a bathroom with another student. That student told investigators Taylor said a tip would be created anonymously and would not be traced back to Taylor, according to the affidavit. Taylor was advised of constitutional rights and agreed to speak with investigators. Taylor's laptop was then confiscated as evidence. The investigation resulted in probable cause to book the student for false report concerning planting a bomb, according to the affidavit. Taylor was taken into custody and transported to the Martin County Sheriff's Office jail before being transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. The original threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The district previously notified families that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said Taylor can only be linked to this specific threat. False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Principal Lori Vogel said, adding that false threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms or other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Boca Raton native Frankie Harris is making a name for himself in professional golf, winning a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his pro career and setting his sights on the PGA Tour.Harris grew up with golf in his blood. Christian McCaffrey put himself in some elite company with two short touchdown runs.McCaffrey's two 1-yard TDs in a 35-13 win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday made him the fourth-fastest player in the Super Bowl era to reach 100 career touchdowns and the third player ever with at least 50 TDs with two franchises.“It means a lot,” McCaffrey said. “It's a blessing to be able to play this game and stuff like that is always cool. Marshall Faulk was somebody that I’ve probably seen every single snap he’s played. I don’t take it for granted. Randy Moss I played with a ton of times with Madden growing up. Those are huge, huge honors.”MORE NFL NEWS | NFL ends the Pro Bowl game, but players will still be honored as Pro BowlersMcCaffrey's career is full of noteworthy accomplishments already. He became the third player ever with at least 1,000 yards rushing and receiving in the same season in 2019 with Carolina, has earned first-team All-Pro honors in three seasons, and won the AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year in 2023 and Comeback Player of the Year in 2025.“It’s crazy. Florida's Treasure Coast earned its name from Spanish coins that washed ashore centuries ago — and the legendary treasure hunters who came to collect them.Melvin Fisher-Abt is the grandson and namesake of one of America's most celebrated treasure hunters, Mel Fisher."I was born in 1997 and Mel passed in 1998 and out of all of the grandkids I was given the namesake Mel and I feel really connected to my grandfather in that way — definitely have big shoes to fill," Fisher-Abt said.His grandfather was a man whose dedication and determination rewrote the history books. His discoveries were so remarkable that Johnny Carson invited him to share his story with millions of viewers on "The Tonight Show.'Mel Fisher walked on stage wearing one of his favorite finds — a gold wedding chain."That's how he would look when he was sitting at the bar — draped in gold chains with gold bars," Fisher-Abt said.But before the fame and fortune came persistence, perseverance, and personal loss.Mel Fisher made his first discovery off the coast of Vero Beach, where over 1,000 gold coins were unearthed from the sunken 1715 Spanish Treasure Fleet."Gold is a noble metal and will be just as shiny as the day it went down — gold shines forever is what my grandfather used to say," Fisher-Abt said.In the 1600s and 1700s, Spanish fleets sailed annually from Spain to the Caribbean with a threefold mission."They were trying to extract wealth from the new world and bring it back to Spain to fund European wars and debts — they were trying to promote Catholicism," Fisher-Abt said. "They were trying to conquer land for the kingdom of Spain — so 'God, Glory and Gold' was their mission."When some of those fleets shipwrecked in major storms, Florida became a hotspot for treasure hunters. One of them — the Spanish galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha — sank in a powerful hurricane in 1622 off the coast of Key West.Mel Fisher moved his family and crew to the Florida Keys specifically to search for the Atocha's buried treasure."Initially, he believed they would find it in six months and after six months he said alright maybe a year — and after a year he said alright maybe we'll be here for awhile," Fisher-Abt said. "He was an eternal optimist."In 1973, Mel Fisher found a 14-foot galleon anchor he believed was from the Atocha."Everyday he would wake up and say today is the day — cause he believed it in his bones that one musket ball and one silver coin and an anchor would lead to a huge pile of treasure," Fisher-Abt said.It was another 12 years before Mel and his team found the massive Atocha "Mother Lode" — an estimated $400 million to $450 million in gold, silver, coins, and emeralds.But before the big find came the greatest test of Mel's determination, when tragedy struck. In 1975, their salvage vessel capsized and three crew members perished, including his eldest son."If there was ever a stopping point that my grandfather really considered giving up the hunt losing my uncle Dirk was that point in time," Fisher-Abt said.Yet Mel chose to honor his son's memory by continuing the quest they shared."When he did get back to the site it was a renewed sense of finishing the job," Fisher-Abt said.He found the Atocha's main treasure pile exactly 10 years to the day after his greatest loss. The search continues to this day."Along the way we've recovered all kinds of artifacts — religious artifacts — some of them are very intricate some are preserved very well deep in the mud," Fisher-Abt said.According to Fisher-Abt, there is still much more to be found."The research that's been done and the work that's been done by the people before us is true and faithful and that everything they've done will pan out for us — there is another 20 tons of silver at the end of the rainbow," Fisher-Abt said.For more information about Mel Fisher's Treasures, click here.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." "We had several young men go out to commit a dangerous, violent act and subsequently shoot and kill someone in their community."The victim and suspects are all from the same general area and may have known each other in passing, but police said they do not believe they were friends. One suspect is 17, and the other two are 16, officials said. All attend schools within the Palm Beach County school system.Because the suspects are minors facing potential capital charges, their names will not be released unless and until they are formally processed through the legal system as adults, police said.
