Calusa Elementary School in Boca Raton broke its own fundraising record at its 15th annual St. Baldrick's event, raising more than $94,000 to help find a cure for childhood cancer.More than 45 teachers and students shaved their heads in solidarity with children battling cancer. On Friday, the school's lunchroom was converted to a barbershop/concert hall for the event.WATCH BELOW: Student cancer survivor leads school's record $94K fundraiser"The St. Baldrick's Foundation is a foundation that raises funds to find a cure for cancer. Kids will shave their heads in solidarity for those kids fighting the battle right now," organizers Jamie Kshonz and Joanne White said.Leading the charge was fifth grader Camden Katz, who raised more than any other participant."$5,000 plus," Katz said.For Katz, the event carries a deeply personal meaning. He was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma in 2024 at age 9."It means a lot. I was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma in 2024 when I was nine," Katz said.Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rare, fast-growing cancer that targets the body's soft tissues, specifically in immature cells intended to develop into skeletal muscle.Katz still has a long road to recovery, even after completing 17 months of chemotherapy in New York. However, he was still able to attend this year's St. Baldrick's event, where he was greeted with chants filling the lunchroom — including his best friend, Gabriel Helitzer."It's great because that's my friend doing brave things up there. Every dollar and every little piece of hair goes to something important for kids like Camden," Helitzer said.Katz said the outpouring of support reinforced why the event matters."It means a lot that I had so much support. It's so important to raise more money to find cures for kids like me; every dollar counts," Katz said.The school's fundraising total was $94,064.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

An anonymous donation expected to exceed $50 million is helping cover tuition costs for medical laboratory science students at the University of Washington for the next half-century.The dean of the university's School of Medicine, Dr. Tim Dellit, made the surprise announcement Monday to about 30 grateful undergrads, who will each see two quarters' worth of tuition covered for their senior-year clinical rotations, The Seattle Times reported."I'm really shocked," said Jasmine Wertz, eyes filling with tears. Extremely grateful."Students in the program are trained to perform clinical lab tests on patient samples, which are used to help diagnose, treat and prevent disease and other conditions. Their clinical rotations are so time-consuming that it's hard to hold down part-time jobs during them.RELATED STORY | Trump Administration details plans to further dismantle Department of EducationThe gift is the latest in a series of recent donations helping pay for college around the country. Last year, the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York received a $1 billion donation from Ruth Gottesman, a former professor and the widow of a Wall Street investor, making tuition there free.Most medical students at Johns Hopkins University no longer pay tuition thanks to a $1 billion gift from Bloomberg Philanthropies.In September at Marshall University in West Virginia, President Brad Smith and his wife, Alys Smith, announced a $50 million gift to promote a program aimed at eliminating student debt, in part by covering tuition for West Virginia students with family income of $65,000 or less.The University of Washington announcement on Monday is worth about $8,000 to $10,000 per student, said UW Medicine spokesperson Susan Gregg. The program will also be able to expand from 70 to 100 students over the next 10 years.The donor, from Washington state, wishes to remain anonymous, but "had a relationship with this program," Gregg said. The donor is also a fan of the local burger chain Dick's, and burgers were piled high atop platters as the students celebrated.ICYMI | Brown University rejects Trump administration's higher education proposalThe field of medical laboratory services has faced increasing demand and an aging workforce in Washington, according to UW Medicine. Those factors have resulted in an "urgent need to grow the pipeline of highly skilled clinical laboratory professionals," the health care system said in a news release."You are the glue, in many ways, of our entire health system," Dellit told the students. "You are the unsung heroes. You work behind the scenes that allow all of the health care machinery to work."

A free private elementary school in West Palm Beach is transforming the lives of at-risk youth through education, with remarkable improvements in reading scores that are catching the attention of the community.Carver Christian Academy, operated by Urban Youth Impact along North Australian Avenue, serves students from some of the area's most challenging circumstances. The school's mission focuses on educating and empowering children who face significant obstacles at home and in their communities.WATCH BELOW: School sees dramatic reading improvements for at-risk students"96% of our students come from a broken family," said Chris Tress, CEO of Urban Youth Impact.The Christian school specifically targets children from areas of concentrated disadvantage, including neighborhoods like Tamarind Avenue (in West Palm Beach) and Riviera Beach. For three decades, Urban Youth Impact has been investing in inner-city children, and their educational approach is yielding impressive results.The school's reading program has produced particularly striking outcomes. Over a 10-year testing period, data showed that only 13% of incoming students could read at grade level at the beginning of each school year. However, by year's end, 77% of those same students achieved grade-level reading proficiency.Recent data revealed even more encouraging trends: 88% of students improved their reading skills over one year63% are now reading at grade level 53% are reading above grade levelThe school's success stems partly from its small class sizes, which allow for individualized attention. Beyond academics, the school focuses on inspiring students to pursue their dreams and providing a safe environment for their development. Teachers and community members work together to mentor students and help them envision positive futures.When asked about his aspirations, one student shared his goal of becoming a pastor, reflecting the school's emphasis on both educational achievement and character development.The combination of academic support, small class sizes and community investment appears to be creating lasting change for students who might otherwise struggle in traditional educational settings.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Even as there are talks of ending the government shutdown, the problems it created are far from over.With SNAP benefits continuing to face uncertainty and groceries still costly, more people are in search of food, especially with the holidays fast approaching.WATCH BELOW: Local church rallies to feed its hungry neighborsBut on Tuesday, WPTV learned how communities are coming together to help their neighbors in need.On Veterans Day, there were reminders that the fight against hunger continues."Last week, we saw a 50% increase (in people using the church pantry)," said Marilyn Lawrence, who oversees the food pantry at Good Shepherd Episcopal Church in Tequesta.Lawrence shared with us paperwork that showed when the COVID-19 pandemic started, their food pantry helped two families a week. Now, that figure is almost 75 families each week."My wife and I are both on Social Security. It's just a blessing with the price of groceries and all that's going on," George Vernon said on Tuesday as church volunteers placed groceries in his car.Rev. Sanford Groff said that with the recent pause on SNAP benefits, they decided to hold a food drive at the church."What happened was an overwhelming response. A very positive outreach so that we can help people in need, serve our neighbors, feed our neighbors," Groff said.What also helped was a push on social media.That amount of support has left the church pantry full, and now it has enough food to feed up to 1,000 people.Groff told WPTV reporter Jon Shainman that while the food drive served a purpose of feeding their neighbors, it also rallied the community."I like to think of it as a way of standing up to the narratives that this world is more divided, more polarized, more at tension with each other," Groff said.The church will continue to host its pantry each Tuesday. Click here to learn more about how you can donate or if you are in need.

Joaquin Garcia High School opened three years ago in western Lake Worth, establishing itself as a formidable football team in Palm Beach County.But starting quarterback Caleb Butler is establishing relationships that will last him and his best friend, Troy Baldwin, for life.WATCH BELOW: Winning season extends beyond the field for Garcia HS quarterbackTwo years ago, Butler arrived on the campus of Garcia High School."I got here at the end of my sophomore year, around the fourth quarter. I've really just grown into the system and the school. The coaching staff and team brought me in as a family," Butler said.Butler is known as the team's leader.However, off the field, Butler has developed a relationship with a teammate who doesn't lace up his cleats."He's cool and we play football," said Butler's best friend, Troy "The QB Stopper" Baldwin.The relationship began two years ago, when Butler joined the school's Best Buddies Program."Me and him, as soon as I saw him, I said, 'Dang, that's going to be a great friend of mine,'" Butler said.The two now spend every day together.You can see them in the classroom making shirts or on the football field, sharpening their skills."I pull up to his games and watch him play. He is a good quarterback," Baldwin said.Two weeks ago, the duo was nominated for the honor of Champion of the Year, a fundraiser through Best Buddies."It's a big impact; it goes straight to Best Buddies. Last year, they made over $200,000, and it was great," Butler said.With two months until Butler early enrolls at the University of North Carolina at Pembroke, WPTV reporter Kendall Hyde asked him if it was bittersweet that he'll soon be leaving Baldwin."A friendship and a bond are something that you can't get rid of. It's still going to stay, and even if I'm miles away, I'll still call Troy and make sure he's OK and know he's my best friend," Butler said.Click here to learn how you can become a part of the Best Buddies program.

Body camera video captured the moments on Sunday morning when a Riviera Beach officer helped a family of four escape their home after their truck caught fire.Officer Andrew Hinds spoke with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache about how it all happened.WATCH BELOW: Officers alert family after truck fire threatens homeHinds called it a case of being at the right place, at the right time."Honestly, I'm just relieved that everybody got out and it didn’t spread anymore," said Hinds.Hinds was on regular patrol duty at about 10 a.m. when he noticed smoke."While we were doing traffic, we looked up and saw smoke coming from a house," said Hinds.Officers rushed towards the house and found a truck engulfed in flames."Residents were flagging us down, telling us there were people inside; some small kids and a family," said Hinds.Hinds was the one to call dispatch and notify them of the truck fire. Officers rushed to the door and began knocking before the fire spread."Your house, look! It's going to be set on fire! Anybody else in the house? Hurry up, get out," Hinds could be heard telling the family inside the home. "Go go go go go!"Hinds said the family of four was asleep and unaware of the flames. His priority was to rush them to safety."Honestly, you could hear the crackling from the car going on fire," said Hinds. "In my mind, I'm like, OK, they probably have gas in there. I don't know how long I have to hurry everybody out. This thing might explode."The family was comforted by neighbors as firefighters put the flames out.Although the truck was destroyed, for Hinds, it's a day when their presence mattered most."I would hate to even think about what would happen if we didn't see the fire," said Hinds. "So it was nice that we just happened to be at the right time at the right place."

A Boca Raton man is bringing light to his community after helping raise money to house a homeless man.John Ferber is behind the good deed and said his act was inspired by a video on social media. Ferber spotted Peter Martin at a bus stop bench months ago and decided to approach him.WATCH BELOW: WPTV's Zitlali Solache speaks with Ferber and Martin"I just had some free time and I decided to grab some Chinese food," said Ferber. “I drove up to Peter and sure enough, he was on the bench where I thought he would be, and we had a great conversation."Ferber learned Martin lost his job back in 2023, leaving him homeless. Ferber started a GoFundMe to help Martin find a studio apartment and quickly raised nearly $4,000."I've gone through a lot, days and days, 5,6,7, days without eating at times," said Martin. Fresh new start."With the funds collected by Ferber, Martin will move into a studio apartment on Wednesday. Martin adds that the gift came just in time, as he celebrated his 67th birthday on Monday."It was my birthday and John pulled up," said Martin. "He hit me with that big gift and never in my life has anybody been that forthcoming and gracious and hospitable, giving generously," said Martin.During his time in the streets, Martin suffered two heart attacks. Martin adds he was once a chef and hopes to get back to his craft."I hope to get the job and use what I've been using for 45-50 years as far as skill and knowledge and bring some value to a business," said Martin.For Ferber, it's only the beginning of his acts of kindness and his friendship with Peter. He hopes his good deed creates a domino effect in his community."Peter, I love you. I know that this is the first step to the best next year and the rest of your life," said Ferber. "I'm glad you're not on that bench anymore, and I'm here with you."The GoFundMe link can be found here.

A simple Facebook post from a Wisconsin mother has grown into an effort to help families at risk of losing their food assistance benefits due to the ongoing federal government shutdown.Rachel Hartberg posted in a private moms group asking if anyone needed food help with SNAP benefits potentially ending. Within hours, dozens of mothers across Waukesha County responded — not asking for help, but offering to donate."I thought maybe a few families would reach out," Hartberg said.Then she went to bed, and the next morning found messages from other mothers wanting to contribute to the cause."Woke up and was like, 'Oh, people actually want to help,'" Hartberg said.The Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program (SNAP), sometimes called food stamps, is 100% federally funded. If the federal government remains shut down, benefits will likely not reach families in need. Megan Zintek, one of Rachel’s friends and among the first to donate, said the situation moved her to tears."We were literally tearing up about it, just thinking about kids being hungry. It almost seemed like an impossible feat," Zintek said. "Here we are having these conversations, Rachel does something about it."Rachel is now spending the day driving around Waukesha County collecting donations from community members. About 30 to 40 people have reached out to offer donations, while 15 families have asked for food assistance.IN RELATED NEWS | SNAP benefits at risk, workers miss pay as shutdown continuesThe need is growing across southeastern Wisconsin. Impact 211, which serves the region, reports an average of 81 requests for food assistance per day since the government shutdown began in October — the highest number in two years.Rachel said the response reflects how women support each other during difficult times."I feel like women stick together," Rachel said. "Bringing people together to make sure people don't go hungry."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.This story was originally published by Rebecca Klopf with the Scripps News Group in Milwaukee.

The WTA Finals, the elite season-ending event in women's tennis, will be held in Charlotte, North Carolina, for the next three years in a move that organizers hope will create "the Super Bowl for women's sports."The tournament will be played at the Spectrum Center, home of the NBA's Charlotte Hornets, the WTA and the Charlotte Sports Foundation announced Wednesday.The year's top eight singles players and doubles teams qualify for the event, which is usually held in November."Our ambition is for the WTA Finals to be not only the premier championship in women's tennis, but one of the defining global events in women sports," WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. "We want to create the Super Bowl for women's sports. And not just the competition, but an event that is the annual gathering for women's tennis, women's sports, and women's sport business.""Audiences are growing, investment is growing, female athletes are increasingly at the center of sports and culture around the world. And women's tennis has helped lead and define that progress for more than 50 years. And we believe our biggest championship should reflect the scale of this moment," Camillo added.Camillo called it a "minimum three-year deal. She added, "We'll see what goes on beyond that."The announcement comes at a time of financial difficulty for the WTA after it announced in July that it was opting out of the final year of a three-year hosting arrangement with Saudi Arabia to move this year's Finals to Indian Wells, California.There were concerns about going back to Saudi Arabia due to military conflicts in the Middle East.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | WTA introduces gene testing for all players on women's tennis tourCamillo noted that "2026 is a year of transition for the WTA" and that "we are doing the normal belt tightening you would expect in any business while also absorbing the unexpected cost of relocating the WTA finals to Indian Wells."What's most important to know is that we have a clear path to deliver consistent, sustainable financial performance in 2027 and beyond," she added.With Indian Wells now set to host only once, Charlotte will become the eighth different venue for the Finals since 2018.The WTA did not announce any prize money figures for the upcoming tournaments, and could struggle to match the record-setting amounts that were on offer in Saudi Arabia.Elena Rybakina collected $5.23 million for winning the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh after going 5-0 at the event. The WTA said that was the largest payout in the history of women's sports. Aryna Sabalenka earned $2.7 million as runner-up.Rybakina also beat Sabalenka in Saturday's U.S. Open final and claimed the No. 1 ranking.Coco Gauff won the 2024 finals in Riyadh.The partnership will extend beyond the Finals. The WTA will also relocate its global headquarters from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Charlotte, as part of the deal.And there's a plan to bring a WTA 500 tournament to Charlotte after 2029."The WTA has always owned the WTA finals, but now going forward, we're going to operate it too," Camillo said. "We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing."And that allows us to control our own destiny," Camillo added. "Whether it's around what we're doing with our media rights and our production, whether it's related to the WTA finals, whether we're approaching our calendar, we're going to be making bold and aggressive moves for women's tennis that shapes the future that we want rather than reacting."RELATED STORY | Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins French Open to become youngest champion since 1992Camillo replaced retiring chair Steve Simon at the end of last year.She previously oversaw business operations for the Philadelphia Flyers and Wells Fargo Center as the president and CEO of the sports and entertainment division of Comcast Spectacor, and has held senior roles with the Washington Nationals and the NBA.Asked if there was a desire to eventually merge with the ATP Finals — the men's season-ending event — Camillo said "there hasn't been an in-depth conversation about merging" the two tournaments."I think that when we create our ambition, people are going to want to merge with us on this event and many more," she added.The move to the Hornets arena during the NBA season means that the Finals will be condensed from eight to five days.That means the traditional schedule of two singles and two doubles matches per day could become four singles and four doubles matches per day."We are exploring a series of alternate formats," Camillo said.The Spectrum Center has already hosted high-profile tennis exhibition events in recent years."As an organization, our mission is quite simple," Will Pitts, CEO of the Charlotte Sports Foundation, said of the Finals. "It's drive economic impact and add to the quality of life through high-profile sporting events and unique partnerships. And this certainly does that."The move comes as Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper is investing an additional $500 million into ongoing stadium renovations with an eye toward potentially bringing the Super Bowl, NFL draft, 2031 Women's World Cup and other major sporting events to Charlotte.

hero.headline: Arsenic hot spot found on Fort Pierce brownfield, not Shelli development site
hero.body:
New state environmental testing results show the most significant arsenic contamination near Fort Pierce's Fisherman's Wharf sits on a separate city brownfield property, not on the waterfront parcel the city sold to developer Chris Shelli, raising questions about the city's earlier claim that contamination could wipe out his damages in an ongoing lawsuit.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection found arsenic about 148 times the residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of a former citrus packing house property immediately north of Fisherman's Wharf. St. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site. On the approximately 3.2-acre development parcel the city sold to Shelli, FDEP found arsenic above residential cleanup targets in only two soil samples, both less than twice the target level.

The city sent Shelli a letter in 2025 arguing the property was likely contaminated and that the cost of remediation essentially eliminates his damages claim. The city made that assertion before FDEP completed its testing. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels associated with the former citrus packing house property but did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.

Jordan Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, reviewed the findings and said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. Beckler said the vast majority of the samples were not that high above the residential standard and noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils.

Shelli sued Fort Pierce for breach of contract after emails showed city commissioners did not learn until 2023, about two years after the sale, that removing a state right-of-reverter restriction on roughly half the property could cost nearly $2 million. The restriction means the land could revert to the state if sold for private development.

Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, said questions could remain over what the city knew or should have known and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before purchase.

Fort Pierce commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli in March. The city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action and the offer was later deemed rejected.

Mike Jenkins, whose family owns the property beneath 12A Buoy restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf and has owned the property for roughly 50 years, said associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. A city spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.

cards.headline: Parking dispute sparked Pollo Tropical shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details.
cards.body:
Christopher Harris, 37, who was shot in the chest at a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical on Saturday, now faces battery and aggravated battery charges despite being the shooting victim, according to newly released incident report details that show the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space.

Multiple witnesses told police they observed Harris push another man and engage in a verbal argument before the man discharged a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris came back inside the restaurant and asked someone to call 911.

A witness picking up an Uber order told police she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.

A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to come outside. The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris ran up on him with a knife.

Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed that Harris, listed as a victim in the report, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three shootings on Avenue L, say suspects identified
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L over four days are connected and targeted. A mother and her four children were inside one home when bullets entered, including rounds that hit her teenage son's bedroom.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects.

The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep."

The family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said she now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Fire at Wendy's on Jensen Beach Boulevard caused by burned-out AC fan motor
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue units responded to a fire at a Wendy's restaurant at 1409 NE Jensen Beach Boulevard in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon. The fire was caused by a burned-out fan motor in an air conditioning unit on the roof. The building was safely evacuated, no injuries were reported, and no nearby structures were threatened.

Units were called to the scene at around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday after reports of smoke and visible flames coming from inside the restaurant, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The emergency call brought firefighters to the location to investigate the source of the smoke and flames that had been reported by witnesses at the scene.

Upon arrival, firefighters found white smoke coming from the AC unit on the roof and light to moderate smoke inside the building. Crews worked to locate the source of the fire and discovered it was the air conditioning unit mounted on the roof of the restaurant. After inspecting the unit, firefighters noticed the fan motor had burned out, which was determined to be the cause of the fire and smoke.

Martin County Fire Rescue successfully extinguished the fire and ensured the building was safe before clearing the scene. The quick response by fire crews prevented the fire from spreading to other parts of the building or threatening nearby structures in the area. No firefighters or civilians were injured during the incident, and the evacuation of the building proceeded without complications.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast voters face local ballot questions Nov. 3 on taxes, services, land
hero.body:
Treasure Coast voters will decide five local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from land protection and mosquito control to sales taxes and trash pickup.

In Martin County, two proposed charter amendments apply only to Stuart voters. One would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve.

St. Lucie County has three local issues. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Port St. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee. The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents' preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change.

A third St. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy.

No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River County. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police identify suspects in three Avenue L shootings that hit homes
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police have identified suspects in three connected shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L, where a mother and her four children were inside during gunfire that hit their house three times within days.

The shootings occurred Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. Evidence shows all three shootings are related, according to police.

"The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

The mother's home was struck first on Tuesday, then twice more on Friday. During the Friday night shooting around 9:07 p.m., multiple bullets entered the house through walls and windows, including rounds that went into her teenage son's bedroom. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the mother said.

Officers found at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother and her children dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their house. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep."

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home.

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Woman faces 9 charges after stolen Broward Sheriff's cruiser found on I-95 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County and deployed K-9 units and a drone to apprehend her over concerns she had access to a firearm. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale, faces nine charges including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, and possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon.

Broward County Regional Communications received a report shortly after 9 p.m. that a marked Broward Sheriff's Office vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.

Deputies spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. Port St. Lucie Police deployed both K-9 units and drone resources. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident.

Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The deputy whose vehicle was stolen was on duty and reported the marked unit missing. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The Broward Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs Unit is investigating to determine what happened and if any agency policy was violated.

cards.headline: Cybersecurity expert finds credit card skimmer on Fort Pierce 7-Eleven pump
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional discovered a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, prompting a police investigation. The expert recommends pulling firmly on card readers and using tap payment or paying inside to avoid theft.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional discovered a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, and the Fort Pierce Police Department is now investigating.

Arlo Bess found the device at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 while stopping for gas before heading back to Palm Bay. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. That background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose.

Bess said skimmers like the one he found are often held on with double-sided tape and take about two to three seconds to install or remove. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online.

Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. The manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company.

Bess said you cannot reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. He said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they cannot be seen at all.

Bess recommends tapping your card or going inside to pay. He said it is much harder to put skimming devices on card readers inside the store. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen.

hero.headline: Martin County High School sophomore arrested in fourth bomb threat in a week
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after making a false bomb threat, the fourth targeting the Stuart school in just over a week, as parents express mounting fear with three earlier threats still unsolved.

Sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida's school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period Tuesday morning, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Surveillance video and student interviews led investigators to Taylor, who later admitted making the false report because he wanted to get out of his third-period class, deputies said. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School.

The repeated threats are taking a toll on families. Freshman Maya and her mother Liz described the fear during school drop-off Wednesday morning. "The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn't even go off," Maya said. "A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary." Liz said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off. "It is very concerning," Liz said. "Every morning it's like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one?"

The Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the three earlier threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. Martin County High School officials said counselors are readily available to support students and emphasized that false threats carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. "False threats and false reports are not pranks," the school said in a statement. "They create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences."

hero.headline: Fort Lauderdale woman charged after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to I-95 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities say she stole a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car from a public safety building and abandoned it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, was arrested following a multi-agency response that included drone surveillance and K-9 units.

Broward County Regional Communications received a report shortly after 9 p.m. that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. Deputies spotted Dillon nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.

Port St. Lucie police established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the department deployed both K-9 units and drone resources. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident.

Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The Broward County Sheriff's Office said nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty and reported his marked unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine what happened and if any agency policy was violated.

hero.headline: Fourth bomb threat in week leads to arrest at Martin County High School
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after making a false bomb threat, the fourth threat targeting the Stuart school in just over a week as parents express mounting anxiety about their children's safety.

Noah Taylor, a sophomore, used FortifyFL to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Taylor later admitted making the false report because he wanted to get out of his third-period class, deputies said. Taylor was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving the school.

The Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the other three threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active.

The repeated threats are taking a toll on students and families. Liz, the mother of freshman Maya, said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. "Every morning it's like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one?" Liz said Wednesday morning.

Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. "The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn't even go off," Maya said. "A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary."

District officials said counselors are readily available to support students who are nervous from the ongoing issue. Martin County High School stated in a release that false threats create fear, disrupt the educational environment, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. The school emphasized that individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable. The school will be providing additional services during the school day, including school social service workers and school counselors. Two school resource officers remain on campus, and additional patrols continue as part of normal daily safety operations.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds holds Stuart roundtable on insurance, taxes six weeks before election
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds met with about a dozen Martin County voters at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart on Wednesday to discuss homeowners insurance, property taxes and healthcare costs.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds met with about a dozen Martin County voters at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart on Wednesday to discuss homeowners insurance, property taxes and healthcare costs with six weeks remaining until the November election.

Rep. Donalds spent about an hour in a small meeting room taking questions from insurance agents, realtors and homeowners rather than delivering a formal speech. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living.

One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes.

When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. On healthcare, Donalds said he wants to address in-network and out-of-network issues and prior authorizations.

Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor.

Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election.

cards.headline: Donalds backs Amendment 3 homestead exemption; Jolly opposes, debate off the table
cards.teaser: Republican Byron Donalds supports Amendment 3's expansion of Florida's homestead tax exemption to $250,000, while Democrat David Jolly opposes the measure and confirmed his decision not to debate Donalds before the November election.
cards.body:
Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly presented opposing positions Wednesday on Amendment 3, the ballot measure that would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption to $250,000 over two years, during the WLRN Sunshine Economy Summit in downtown Fort Lauderdale.

Donalds told the audience he supports the measure. "I think voters need relief. I think the property owners need relief," Donalds said. Jolly said he anticipates voting against Amendment 3. "I don't think the math works, and I think we know that because even Ron DeSantis now won't campaign for Amendment 3, and our sheriffs have come out and said, 'Please don't do this. It's going to defund services,'" Jolly said. The two gubernatorial nominees spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions but were kept separate throughout the event.

The candidates also clashed on hurricane insurance reform. Jolly proposed a sovereign wealth fund that would absorb hurricane and wind insurance burdens for Floridians. "We are not going to solve this without government taking on a larger role in backing this. Otherwise, people are going to be priced out of their homes," Jolly said. Donalds said that plan won't work and instead called for eliminating a premium surcharge that contributes to the state's catastrophic fund. "We get through this hurricane season, the Cat Fund is estimated to have somewhere between 13 and 13-and-a-half billion dollars. So why do we have a 25% kicker on top to keep filling the Cat Fund, whose statutory limit is $17 billion? My view is to get rid of the kicker. That would lower premiums for every policyholder in the state," Donalds said.

Jolly confirmed earlier this week he will not debate Donalds, making this the first gubernatorial election in 50 years in which Florida voters won't see the nominees face off. "It just became obvious that this is not going to contribute to a more constructive political environment, and that's the bottom line. I understand some people have concerns about it. I just promise you, for me, this is a moment bigger than politics," Jolly told reporters after his panel discussion. Donalds said he wants the debate to happen. "He said something about how I lied about him — which is a lie, by the way — and so he doesn't want to debate. Well, that's what debates are for: to clarify all that stuff. The ball's in his court," Donalds said. When asked if his decision could change, Jolly said his decision is final. Both candidates share a commitment to keeping Florida free of a state income tax.

hero.headline: Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stolen Broward patrol vehicle found on I-95 in St. Lucie County
hero.teaser: A Fort Lauderdale woman is in the St. Lucie County Jail after a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was found abandoned on an Interstate 95 off-ramp Tuesday night.
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman is in the St. Lucie County Jail after a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was found abandoned on an Interstate 95 off-ramp Tuesday night, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Deputies, Port St. Lucie police officers and Florida Highway Patrol troopers went to I-95 at about 9:40 p.m. Tuesday after receiving information that a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was heading north near Gatlin Boulevard. The response was coordinated with the Broward Sheriff's Office. When units arrived, they found the patrol vehicle abandoned on the Gatlin Boulevard off-ramp.

Deputies then saw a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest with Broward Sheriff's Office insignia on it. They stopped her and identified her as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale.

In St. Lucie County, Dillon faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges in Broward County of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to the sheriff's office.

Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

cards.headline: Three Avenue L shootings targeting Fort Pierce homes are connected, police say
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police confirmed three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, with investigators having already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18, according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

The mother, who asked not to be identified, said her home was struck three times within days. Bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. The mother said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible.

"I have little kids and they are terrified," the mother said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep. I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do."

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. Friday. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house," the girl said. "With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house. If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA offers bulk tree program as Sept. 30 deadline nears in Cadence at Tradition dispute
cards.teaser: The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to join its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees, even as homeowners continue to dispute responsibility for trees on swales.
cards.body:
The Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association is offering residents a chance to participate in its bulk tree-purchase program as the Sept. 30 deadline approaches for replacing dead trees in the community. Homeowners in the Port St. Lucie community received notices dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding dead trees on their property be replaced by Sept. 30 or face escalation, but many residents say the trees are on swales and should be the HOA's responsibility.

A public relations firm for The Cadence at Tradition HOA said the association is replacing thousands of dead trees and shrubs in common areas that have yet to recover from the last freeze. The firm said residents are responsible for replacing trees in limited common areas such as rights of way immediately adjacent to and between individual lots, including areas containing sidewalks and driveway aprons. Because the HOA is purchasing and installing trees in bulk, it has invited residents to participate in the program. The program allows homeowners to share in the cost savings while ensuring tree replacements around their homes are selected and installed professionally, according to the statement.

Homeowner Chip Collison said the dead trees were in common areas, not in yards, and he wants the HOA to pay for new trees in the swales. Keyla Peguero, another homeowner at Cadence at Tradition, said she replaced a dead tree in the swale in front of her house at a total cost of $300 to remove the dead tree, haul it away and replace it. She said she is not willing to do it again and should not have had to do it in the first place.

The HOA has removed many of the dead trees, leaving holes in the ground where residents are supposed to put in new trees at the homeowners' expense. Some residents say new trees should be planted in April at the start of the growing season rather than now. Collison said if new trees are planted now during hurricane season, a strong hurricane could destroy them and they would have to be redone again. The Sept. 1 notice from Campbell Property Management does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not replace the dead trees by the deadline.

hero.headline: 15-year-old arrested for fourth bomb threat at Martin County High School in a week
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after making a false bomb threat, the fourth threat targeting the Stuart school in just over a week, as parents voice mounting concern over school safety.

Sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL, Florida's school safety reporting system, to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period Tuesday morning, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor, who later admitted making the false report because he wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats.

The three earlier threats remain under investigation. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active.

The repeated threats are taking a toll on families. Freshman Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. "The last bomb threat, it was crazy because, like a cop in Building Two, the alarm didn't even go off," Maya said. "A police officer had to go door to door and come get us and tell us to get out of the building. So, it was kind of like scary." Her mother, Liz, said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. "It is very concerning," Liz said. "Every morning it's like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one?"

District officials said counselors are readily available to support students who are nervous from the ongoing issue. Martin County High School officials said false threats create fear, disrupt the educational environment, divert critical law enforcement resources, and carry serious disciplinary and criminal consequences. The school said individuals who make false reports should expect to be held fully accountable.

hero.headline: Florida renter costs could jump hundreds annually under Amendment 3, report finds
hero.body:
A Florida Housing Coalition report released this week estimates that Amendment 3, which would expand the homestead exemption for property owners, could increase annual property taxes by an average of $406 per apartment and $1,081 per single-family rental home in 2028 if local governments raise tax rates to replace lost revenue. Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The exemption reduces the property value on which taxes are calculated for qualifying primary residences, but rental properties do not qualify for the homestead exemption.

Much of the additional tax expense on rental properties could ultimately be passed on to tenants through higher rents, according to Jared Walczak, the tax-policy analyst who wrote the report. "Renters pay taxes, they just don't write the check," Walczak said. "While landlords would write the check, most of the burden would ultimately be borne by renters in the form of higher rent."

The report models what would happen if local governments facing lost revenue respond by increasing property-tax rates to replace that revenue, subject to existing limits on those rates. By 2031, the additional annual property-tax burden would reach $544 per apartment and $1,471 per single-family rental home under the same approach, the report estimates. How much of that cost reaches tenants would depend on rental-market conditions and local budget decisions.

The amendment also includes a provision benefiting rental and other non-homestead properties by lowering the annual cap on increases in assessed value from 10% to 5%. Walczak's report concludes that the benefit of the lower assessment cap would be outweighed by the modeled tax shift. Supporters, including Florida Realtors, argue that homeowners also need help with housing costs. "Everywhere you look, people are feeling the pinch of affordability, and Amendment 3 has the opportunity to return more money back to the taxpayer," said Margy Grant of Florida Realtors.

The potential loss of local revenue has drawn opposition from the Florida Sheriffs Association, which warns the amendment could squeeze funding for deputies and other public-safety needs. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz pushed back against those warnings in a statement posted on X. "Tax relief and public safety are not competing priorities," she said, urging government agencies to examine their spending and eliminate unnecessary costs while protecting essential law-enforcement resources.

Gov. Ron DeSantis supports Amendment 3 and says future lawmakers will pursue targeted state grants to help maintain essential services. "We will ensure that essential services continue, but we also recognize taxpayers need a break," DeSantis said. The proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% of the votes cast on it to pass in November.

hero.headline: Fort Lauderdale woman arrested near stolen Broward Sheriff patrol vehicle on I-95 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman is in the St. Lucie County Jail after a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was found abandoned on an Interstate 95 off-ramp Tuesday night, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

St. Lucie County deputies, Port St. Lucie police officers and Florida Highway Patrol troopers went to I-95 at about 9:40 p.m. after receiving information that a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle was heading north near Gatlin Boulevard. The response was coordinated with the Broward Sheriff's Office.

When units arrived, they found the patrol vehicle abandoned on the Gatlin Boulevard off-ramp. Deputies then saw a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest with Broward Sheriff's Office insignia on it. They stopped her and identified her as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale.

In St. Lucie County, Dillon faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges in Broward County of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

cards.headline: Three connected shootings hit Fort Pierce homes with families inside
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police confirmed Tuesday that three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened September 15 and twice more on September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. Major Mike Santiago said the means and methods used, the types of weapons, and the shooting patterns are all similar in all of the cases. Santiago said the particular homes and the people involved do have histories and that is how investigators are starting to develop the case as it unfolds.

A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. The mother said it was pretty close because if her son would have jumped he would have been hit. Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. The mother said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. The mother said her little kids are terrified and any noise keeps them from sleeping. According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday.

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The girl said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. She said she turned around and they just went shooting and she tried to run in the house. With it raining that day she ended up falling on the floor and when she fell on the floor that is when the bullet went in the house. She said if she did not fall, she would have been hit. The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Cybersecurity expert finds credit card skimmer on Fort Pierce 7-Eleven gas pump
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional discovered an active credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 in Fort Pierce. Police are investigating and recommend consumers tap cards or pay inside.
cards.body:
A man with 25 years of cybersecurity experience found a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, and police are now investigating. Arlo Bess discovered the device at the store on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 when he stopped for gas before heading back to Palm Bay.

Bess said his cybersecurity background made him cautious at the pump. He has tugged on the outside of card readers every time he pays at a gas station for years. This was the first time one came loose. Bess said skimmers take two to three seconds to install and the same amount of time to remove. The devices are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in.

Bess said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. Officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with Bess for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating.

Bess said consumers cannot reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. He said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands without using tools. Newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot where they cannot be seen at all. Bess recommends tapping your card or going inside to pay. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump because fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, and it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby because outdoor machines are easier targets.

Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose. "I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said. Bess said skimmers take almost no time to put on. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. Bess said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating. Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all. "My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie HOA gives Cadence at Tradition homeowners Sept. 30 deadline to replace dead trees
cards.teaser: Residents in the Cadence at Tradition community received letters from their homeowners association demanding they replace dead trees by Sept. 30 or face escalation. Homeowners say the trees are on easements and should be the HOA's responsibility.
cards.body:
Residents in Cadence at Tradition in Port St. Lucie received a letter dated Sept. 1 from Campbell Property Management on behalf of Cadence at Tradition Homeowners Association Inc. demanding they replace dead trees on their property by Sept. 30 or face escalation. The letter does not say what action will be taken if a homeowner does not comply.

The letter states that assistance and cooperation are requested regarding landscaping and dead trees. Residents say the trees are on the easement, the strip of grass between the sidewalk and the street, and were killed during a cold snap. Because the dead trees are on the easement, some residents say it should be the HOA's job to replace them at the HOA's expense, not the homeowners.

Some residents say now is not the best time to replace the dead trees. They say if new trees need to be planted, it should be done in April, at the start of the growing season. Some say if new trees are planted now, they could be wiped out by a freeze in the months ahead.

The letter states that the deceased tree or trees on their property are in need of attention and kindly requests residents address the matter by Sept. 30 to avoid escalation.

hero.headline: Fourth bomb threat in week hits Martin County High; 15-year-old arrested
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after making a false bomb threat through Florida's school safety reporting system, marking the fourth threat to the Stuart school in just over a week as parents express growing anxiety about their children's safety.

Sophomore Noah Taylor used FortifyFL to submit a report claiming bombs were inside a boys bathroom and would go off during third period Tuesday morning, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The school resource deputy determined the threat was not credible. Investigators said surveillance video and interviews with students led them to Taylor, who later admitted making the false report because he wanted to get out of his third-period class. Taylor was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. Sheriff John Budensiek said Taylor is not believed to be connected to the three previous threats involving Martin County High School.

The repeated threats are taking a toll on students and families. Freshman Maya described the response to one of the previous threats as frightening. A police officer had to go door to door in Building Two and tell students to get out of the building after an alarm did not sound. Her mother, Liz, said the string of threats has left her questioning what could happen each time she drops her daughter off at school. "Every morning it's like, should I bring her to school today? Is it going to be another one? Is this going to be the real one?" Liz said. Maya said what initially felt unusual has started to feel more routine after so many incidents. "A lot of people were screaming and calling their parents. Then, when they got home, they were looking on Facebook because Facebook has everything. We all talked about it and who we think is doing it. Everyone was saying it was Russia or something, but I don't know," Maya said.

The Sheriff's Office continues to investigate the three earlier threats. Budensiek said investigators traced the first threat to someone in Russia. The other two investigations remain active. District officials said counselors are readily available to support students if they are nervous from the ongoing issue. The sheriff has warned students that false threats can carry serious and lasting consequences, including criminal charges and possible school discipline. Students returned to class as usual Wednesday.
