hero.headline: Jolly confirms no debate with Donalds in first Florida governor's race without one in 50 years
hero.body:
Democrat David Jolly confirmed this week that he will not debate Republican Byron Donalds in Florida's gubernatorial race, making this the first election in 50 years in which the state's voters will not see the nominees face off. The announcement came as the two candidates clashed over Amendment 3, which would raise the homestead tax exemption to $250,000 over two years, and hurricane insurance reform at the WLRN Sunshine Economy Summit in downtown Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday.

Jolly told reporters after his panel discussion that his decision is final. "It just became obvious that this is not going to contribute to a more constructive political environment, and that's the bottom line. I understand some people have concerns about it. I just promise you, for me, this is a moment bigger than politics," Jolly said.

Donalds said he wants the debate to happen. "He said something about how I lied about him — which is a lie, by the way — and so he doesn't want to debate," Donalds said in response to questions following his panel. "Well, that's what debates are for: to clarify all that stuff. The ball's in his court."

The two candidates spoke in back-to-back 30-minute panel discussions but were kept separate throughout the event. One of the sharpest divides came over Amendment 3, which Florida voters will decide this November. Donalds said he supports the measure. "I think voters need relief. I think the property owners need relief," Donalds said. Jolly said he anticipates he will vote against Amendment 3. "I don't think the math works, and I think we know that because even Ron DeSantis now won't campaign for Amendment 3, and our sheriffs have come out and said, 'Please don't do this. It's going to defund services,'" Jolly said.

Disaster relief and insurance costs also emerged as a major point of contrast. Jolly is proposing a sovereign wealth fund that would absorb hurricane and wind insurance burdens for Floridians. "We are not going to solve this without government taking on a larger role in backing this. Otherwise, people are going to be priced out of their homes," Jolly said. Donalds said that plan will not work. He is instead calling for the elimination of a premium surcharge that contributes to the state's catastrophic fund. "We get through this hurricane season, the Cat Fund is estimated to have somewhere between 13 and 13-and-a-half billion dollars. So why do we have a 25% kicker on top to keep filling the Cat Fund, whose statutory limit is $17 billion? My view is to get rid of the kicker. That would lower premiums for every policyholder in the state," Donalds said.

Despite their differences, both candidates share at least one position: a commitment to keeping Florida free of a state income tax.

hero.headline: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County on I-95
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County, triggering a multi-agency response. Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, was taken into custody after deputies found her near the abandoned vehicle wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.

The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger traveling northbound on I-95. Around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol responded after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Florida Highway Patrol located the abandoned patrol vehicle within minutes on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118.

Dillon faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.

The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

cards.headline: Martin County High student arrested in fourth bomb threat in under two weeks
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat to skip class, marking the fourth threat against the school in less than two weeks. The sheriff warned more arrests may follow as investigators continue probing three other recent threats.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident marks the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half, six weeks into the academic year.

The student told investigators he "was just tired of being in class" and "just wanted to get out of third-period class," Sheriff John Budensiek said. The school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. The tip claimed someone overheard students in the boys bathroom saying there were bombs in the school that would blow up during third period, along with a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus. The student initially denied involvement and claimed someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed.

The student was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services in Fort Pierce. Budensiek said the arrest is not connected to the three other recent threats against the school. The initial threat came through Russia, and investigators are still probing the last two threats. "We could potentially be making some more arrests on that case," Budensiek said.

Budensiek issued a stern warning to students considering similar pranks. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

hero.headline: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer at Fort Pierce 7-Eleven gas pump
hero.teaser: A man with 25 years of cybersecurity experience discovered a credit card skimmer attached to a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, prompting a police investigation.
hero.body:
A cybersecurity professional discovered a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven, and the Fort Pierce Police Department is now investigating.

Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose.

"I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said.

Bess said skimmers take almost no time to install. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. He said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online.

Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company.

Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all.

"My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said.

He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings, identify suspects in targeted attacks on homes
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. Major Mike Santiago said the means and methods used, the shooting, and the types of weapons used are all similar in all of these cases. He said the particular homes and people involved have histories, which investigators are using to develop the case. Santiago said it is a matter of drilling down on details to develop enough probable cause.

Officers responded to a home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes were visible in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. Bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom. The teen's mother said if he would have jumped he would have got hit. She said her little kids are terrified and that any noise keeps her from sleeping.

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she was outside when the gunfire erupted and narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The girl, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she tried to run in the house and ended up falling on the floor when it was raining that day. She said the bullet went in the house when she fell, and that if she did not fall, she would have got hit.

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough and that she now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: No charges in Indiantown bus stop gun incident; two teens dispute sheriff's account
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek closed the investigation into a confrontation at an Indiantown school bus stop Friday without filing charges, determining that a father who pulled a gun on two teenagers acted lawfully under Florida's Stand Your Ground law. The two teenagers involved dispute the sheriff's account and question why an armed adult came to confront juveniles at a bus stop.

The incident occurred Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students prepared to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. Budensiek said the father went to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the previous day. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old brought pizza onto the bus and the 14-year-old began asking for some, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused.

Budensiek said Friday morning the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father, and students on the bus called another 16-year-old to come to the scene. The sheriff said both teenagers approached the father despite repeated warnings to stay back. The father initially held his hand up and told the teenagers to stay back, then pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he is legally allowed to do, Budensiek said. Both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away, and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what happened.

RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory, the two teenagers who confronted the father, told a different version of events. McIntyre said he was called to the bus stop because someone said an old man was looking for him. He said the bus driver eventually told him and the father's son to get off the bus and they appeared ready to fight. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because his younger brother called him and said a grown man was looking for somebody. Ivory said he told the father to let the two teenagers fight, then the father put his son behind him and pulled a gun. McIntyre said when he saw the gun he thought about whether he would make it home. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away.

McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student Thursday but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said he asked if he could buy a slice of pizza for a dollar and the student screamed in his face. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student during the ride home and acknowledged using profanity. McIntyre said no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there are children. The sheriff said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus.

Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident and interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to press charges. The father did not want to press charges and has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. The sheriff said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. Budensiek also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media, saying it did not show the entire context and created confusion in the community.

The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. cards.headline: Martin County High student arrested for fourth bomb threat in under two weeks
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after confessing he sent a fake bomb threat to skip class, marking the fourth threat against the school in less than two weeks.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after confessing he sent a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app to skip class, marking the fourth threat against the school in a week and a half. The student, sophomore Noah Taylor, told investigators he was just tired of being in class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

The school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip stated someone walking by the boys bathroom heard people saying there were bombs in the school that would blow up during third period. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus. Taylor initially denied involvement and claimed someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed and said he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to Sheriff John Budensiek.

The arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against Martin County High School. The initial threat came through Russia, Budensiek said. Investigators are still pursuing the last two threats and could potentially make additional arrests.

Taylor was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services in Fort Pierce. He faces strong repercussions from the school, potentially including expulsion. Budensiek issued a stern warning to students considering similar actions. This really is catastrophic for your life, he said. This individual has been arrested for a felony and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious.

The school district is six weeks into the academic year.

hero.headline: Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County on I-95
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County, where deputies found her wearing tactical gear with sheriff's insignia.

Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, now faces numerous felony charges across two counties. Authorities issued a BOLO alert at 9:30 p.m. for the stolen Dodge Charger traveling northbound on I-95.

At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118.

St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Dillon in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.

The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings, identify suspects
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police confirm three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L over four days are connected and targeted. Investigators have already identified suspects in the case that sent one mother and her four children to the floor as bullets tore through their home.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L between September 15 and September 18 are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

Officers responded to one home around 9:07 p.m. Friday and found multiple bullet holes outside, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. At least 10 bullet holes marked the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. Bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," she said. According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire.

A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit."

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. "I have little kids and they are terrified. Any noise...I can't even sleep." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie advances $2.2 billion 2050 Mobility Plan with phased fee hikes
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, updating mobility fees on developers over the next four years as part of a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that still faces a $1.7 billion funding gap.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, updating mobility fees on developers over the next four years as part of a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that still faces a $1.7 billion funding gap. The plan serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050, including new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. Final approval is required before the plan takes effect on Dec. 31.

The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers. Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the challenge growth presents to city finances during the meeting. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said.

The city remains $1.7 billion short of full funding for the plan. A city official addressed the gap during the council meeting. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said.

Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid-, and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. "Mobility fees may need to supplement that," Samples said.

More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020. Resident Laura Milsom said the growth is impossible to ignore on local roads. "The population increased so rapidly," Milsom said. "A lot of traffic backups." Milsom said she supports requiring developers to help fund infrastructure. "Anyone wanting to come in and develop in the area should be partly responsible for how the traffic is managed and everything," Milsom said.

hero.headline: Martin County High School student arrested for bomb threat; told classmate FortifyFL tip couldn't be traced
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat through the FortifyFL school safety reporting system, later admitting he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore, was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the threat was submitted around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday. Sheriff John Budensiek said the message read, "I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today."

The school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school. Surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. Another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him, according to an affidavit.

Investigators said Taylor initially blamed other students but could not provide identifying information about them. He eventually admitted making the report. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class," Budensiek said. Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before transporting him to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce.

The arrest marks the fourth bomb threat connected to Martin County High School in just over a week and a half. Investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating," the sheriff said.

School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. Principal Lori Vogel said false threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement.

Budensiek warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is," Budensiek said. The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

hero.headline: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County on I-95
hero.body:
A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County, triggering a multi-agency pursuit and a temporary ramp closure.

Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.

The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard.

Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Dillon in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.

The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

cards.headline: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat to skip class
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday on a felony charge after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app because he wanted to get out of class. The incident marks the fourth threat against the school in just over a week.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he was just tired of being in class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.

The school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip said someone walking by the boys bathroom heard students saying there were bombs in the school that would blow up in third period, according to Sheriff John Budensiek. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus. When first confronted, the student denied involvement and said maybe somebody else sent the tip. After further questioning, the student confessed and said he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to the sheriff.

The arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against the school. The initial threat came in through Russia, Budensiek said. Investigators are still working on the last two threats and could potentially make more arrests.

Budensiek issued a warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke. This really is catastrophic for your life, he said. The student has been arrested for a felony and transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He will face strong repercussions from the school, including possible expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious, Budensiek said.

The school district is only six weeks into the academic year.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council approves first reading of $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B gap
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading Monday of the 2050 Mobility Plan, a $2.2 billion infrastructure proposal that updates the city's mobility fee schedule for the next four years and outlines a 25-year vision for roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. The plan faces a $1.7 billion funding gap and requires final council approval before taking effect Dec. 31. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, driving the need for expanded infrastructure to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid population growth.

The city acknowledged during the council meeting that the plan cannot fully fund all needed projects through 2050. A city official said the mobility plan is intended to identify infrastructure needs based on current analysis through 2050 but cannot solve all the problems funding-wise. The official said the plan is a piece of the puzzle. Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the challenge growth presents to city finances, saying growth has never paid for itself.

The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said mobility fees are one of the tools in the city's toolbox to help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure needed to maintain and grow. Resident Laura Milsom said the population increased rapidly and has caused traffic backups. Milsom said anyone wanting to come in and develop in the area should be partly responsible for how the traffic is managed and everything.

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-term, mid-term and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. Samples said mobility fees may need to supplement that project. Milsom said the traffic situation has become difficult to ignore on local roads as rapid expansion has come with consequences. The updated plan still requires final approval from the City Council before taking effect on Dec. 31.

hero.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny praised for rescue of missing woman in Gadsden County
hero.body:
An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his bloodhound partner who helped find a missing 84-year-old woman with dementia in Gadsden County last month have returned home to praise from their agency for responding to the mutual-aid call while away for training. Deputy Sam Lewis and K9 Penny joined bloodhound search teams from across the state in Gadsden County near Tallahassee, where they were attending a K9 certification course when Margaret Myles Ellis was reported missing on Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before.

Officials said Ellis had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Multiple dogs participated in the rotated search effort, with Penny and other bloodhounds taking turns searching for the missing woman. Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area to assist in the search. Ellis was found approximately 30 hours later in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety.

Lt. Eric Jaworski of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office praised Deputy Lewis for responding to the emergency despite being nine counties away. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Jaworski said. He emphasized that Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny were fortunate to be in the right place at the right time. "Luckily, they were at the right place at the right time. We're extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and our entire K9 unit that, you know, goes out every day," Jaworski said.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office K9 unit includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. Jaworski also highlighted the unique role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies within the agency. "Dogs don't judge you, you know they love everybody, so it's a good way to connect and it opens up the door to express some of these things that we see and hear every day," he said. Ellis was reunited with her family following the rescue, and Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned to Indian River County and resumed their regular duties.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council advances $2.2 billion 2050 Mobility Plan on first reading
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that includes an updated mobility fee schedule and a 25-year vision for roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that includes an updated mobility fee schedule and a 25-year vision for roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. The plan requires final approval from the City Council before taking effect on Dec. 31.

The plan serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050 to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid population growth. The city acknowledged the plan remains $1.7 billion short of full funding.

Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the challenge growth presents to city finances. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said.

The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees, which are applied to new development and paid by developers. The updated plan includes a mobility fee schedule for the next four years. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

A city official addressed the funding gap during the council meeting. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said.

The city said more than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020. The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid-, and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes.

Resident Laura Milsom said the growth is impossible to ignore on local roads. "The population increased so rapidly," Milsom said. "A lot of traffic backups." Milsom said she supports the fee approach. "Anyone wanting to come in and develop in the area should be partly responsible for how the traffic is managed and everything," Milsom said.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police confirm three Avenue L shootings striking homes are linked and targeted
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. Major Mike Santiago said the means and methods used, the shooting, and the types of weapons used are all similar in all of these cases. He said it is a matter of drilling down on some of these details to develop enough probable cause. Santiago said the particular homes and the people involved have histories, which is how investigators are starting to develop the case.

A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for bomb threat, fourth in 10 days
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, the fourth threat against the school in just over a week. The student, identified as Noah Taylor, told investigators he was just tired of being in class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip claimed someone was walking by the boys bathroom and overheard talk of bombs in the school that would blow up in third period. The tipster also reported hearing about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to Taylor, who initially denied involvement and suggested someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed and explained he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to Budensiek.

Taylor was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services in Fort Pierce. The arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against Martin County High School. The initial threat came through Russia, Budensiek said, and the last two remain under investigation with more arrests potentially forthcoming.

Budensiek issued a warning to students considering similar threats. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

The arrest comes six weeks into the academic year as authorities signal that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.

cards.headline: More than 1,000 volunteers turn out for Martin County beach cleanup
cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.

Keep Martin Beautiful is the local coordinator of the International Coastal Cleanup. The nonprofit volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful.

County volunteers participated at 28 locations, including Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris. Linda Emerson said at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island that by picking up pieces of plastic, volunteers can realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

cards.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny rescue missing woman in Gadsden County
cards.teaser: Deputy Sam Lewis and bloodhound Penny helped locate an 84-year-old woman with dementia in shallow water after 30 hours missing while attending K9 training near Tallahassee.
cards.body:
An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his bloodhound partner helped rescue an 84-year-old woman with dementia in Gadsden County after the woman had been missing for 30 hours. Deputy Sam Lewis and K9 Penny were attending a K9 certification course near Tallahassee when they joined the search effort for Margaret Myles Ellis.

Ellis was reported missing Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before. She had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Bloodhound search teams from across the state participated in the search, rotating dogs through the effort.

Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area. Ellis was found in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety. "They're coming out," the body camera footage captured.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the deputy's response. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Sheriff Eric Flowers said. He expressed pride in the entire K9 unit, which includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. Ellis was reunited with her family. Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned home and resumed their duties.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council advances $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B funding gap
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid growth through 2050. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years but still faces a $1.7 billion funding shortfall. Final approval is required before the plan takes effect Dec. 31.

The 25-year plan outlines new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit projects. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, and Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge that growth presents. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said. Mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners, fund the infrastructure projects. Scott Samples with the city said increasing mobility fees is one tool to help fund future projects. A city official told the council the plan cannot solve all funding problems but identifies needs through 2050 based on current analysis.

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-term, mid-term and long-term projects. Short-term projects through 2030 include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. Samples said mobility fees may need to supplement that project. The official explained that while the city knows there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, the plan is intended to identify needs through 2050 based on current analysis and serves as one piece of the funding puzzle.

Resident Laura Milsom said the population increased rapidly and has caused traffic backups. She said the community is not in love with the traffic situation and noted the rapid expansion has come with consequences. Milsom said anyone wanting to develop in the area should be partly responsible for how traffic is managed. The plan serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050 as the city works to accommodate continued growth while managing significant funding constraints.

The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years but still faces a $1.7 billion funding shortfall. Final approval is required before the plan takes effect Dec. 31.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

Rehki Jyquan Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge following the stop near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21.

A deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier. Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings, identify suspects
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police have confirmed that three shootings along Avenue L are connected and targeted, with investigators already identifying suspects as they work to develop probable cause for arrests. The shootings occurred on Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18, striking several homes including one where a mother and her four children lived.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

The mother whose home was struck three times within days said bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom during the Friday night shooting around 9:07 p.m. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," she said. Officers found at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home, with several rounds penetrating walls and windows. The woman said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said.

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she was outside when the gunfire erupted and narrowly escaped being struck. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home.

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. No one was hurt in any of the shootings.

hero.headline: Martin County High sophomore Noah Taylor charged with felony for false bomb threat
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School sophomore was arrested Tuesday after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat through the school safety app because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present at the school. The message read, "I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," Sheriff John Budensiek said during a news conference.

The school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and began investigating. Surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. Another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. When questioned, Taylor initially blamed other students but could not provide identifying information about them and eventually admitted making the report. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class," Budensiek said. Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before transporting him to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce.

The arrest marks the fourth threat connected to Martin County High School in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating," the sheriff said. Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact of false threats in a statement. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences, including possible expulsion and difficulty finding employment. The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

cards.headline: Palm City SWAT standoff: Arrest report details Darrel Abbey's gun threats, prison comment
cards.teaser: New arrest report details from the Martin County Sheriff's Office reveal that Darrel Abbey pointed a gun at his ex-girlfriend multiple times, threatened to kill her and her stepfather, and stated he would not return to prison before the hours-long standoff.
cards.body:
An arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office released following an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City reveals that Darrel Abbey pointed a gun at his ex-girlfriend multiple times, threatened to kill her and her stepfather, and said he was not going back to prison.

The ex-girlfriend arrived at Abbey's home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated, according to the report.

Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman while holding a gun. He pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed. Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. When Abbey picked up the gun again, he said it was really dangerous now.

Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. He walked outside and the woman heard several loud pop sounds. Abbey returned inside to retrieve a rifle and tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it.

At some point, Abbey began cleaning the firearms and said he had to wipe all his fingerprints off and get the gunshot residue off of his hands because he was not going back to prison. Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink. The woman began recording him. Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her.

Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for bomb threat to skip class, sheriff says
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday on a felony charge after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The arrest marks the fourth threat against the school in 10 days.

Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip claimed someone overheard talk of bombs in the school set to explode during third period, including a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus.

The student initially denied involvement and suggested someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed that he just wanted to get out of third-period class, Budensiek said. The student was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services facility in Fort Pierce.

Budensiek confirmed the arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against Martin County High School. The first threat came through Russia, he said, and investigators are still working the last two cases with potential additional arrests. The school district is six weeks into the academic year.

Budensiek issued a warning to students considering similar threats. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

cards.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny help rescue missing Gadsden County woman
cards.teaser: Deputy Sam Lewis and his bloodhound partner Penny joined a multi-county search that located an 84-year-old woman with dementia in shallow water after 30 hours missing.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Sam Lewis and his K9 partner Penny helped rescue an 84-year-old woman with dementia during a search in Gadsden County near Tallahassee. The deputy and his bloodhound were attending a K9 certification course when they joined the effort to locate Margaret Myles Ellis, who had been missing for approximately 30 hours.

Ellis was last seen at her home on Sept. 14 and reported missing on Sept. 15. She had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured him scaling down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area during the search. Ellis was found in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety.

Bloodhound search teams from across the state participated in the effort. Penny searched along with other dogs in a rotated dog search, according to officials. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised Lewis and the department's K9 unit for their willingness to help no matter where they are. The sheriff's office K9 unit includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy.

Ellis was reunited with her family after the rescue. Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned to Indian River County and resumed their duties. Sheriff's officials highlighted the role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies, noting that dogs provide a way for law enforcement to connect and express the experiences they encounter daily. The sheriff said the department is extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and the entire K9 unit that goes out every day.

He expressed pride in the entire K9 unit, which includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. "Luckily, they were at the right place at the right time. We're extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and our entire K9 unit that, you know, goes out every day," Jaworski said. Jaworski also highlighted the unique role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies. "Dogs don't judge you, you know they love everybody, so it's a good way to connect and it opens up the door to express some of these things that we see and hear every day," he said. Ellis was reunited with her family, and Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned home and resumed their duties. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council approves $2.2 billion mobility plan on first reading
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council on Monday approved the first reading of a $2.2 billion mobility plan designed to address traffic congestion and accommodate population growth through 2050, though the city faces a $1.7 billion funding gap. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years and outlines a 25-year vision for infrastructure development. The updated plan requires final council approval before taking effect on Dec. 31.

The 2050 Mobility Plan serves as a road map for infrastructure projects including new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, creating visible traffic problems on local roads. Resident Laura Milsom said the population increased rapidly and caused traffic backups. Short-term projects looking ahead to 2030 include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes.

Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge facing the city. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said. The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners. Milsom said she supports that approach, stating that anyone wanting to develop in the area should be partly responsible for how traffic is managed. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

Despite the mobility fee structure, the city says the plan is still $1.7 billion short of full funding. A city official addressed the gap during the council meeting, explaining that the plan cannot solve all problems from a funding perspective but represents one piece of the puzzle. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said. The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-term, mid-term and long-term projects to accommodate continued growth in the city.
