hero.headline: Execution date set for Oct. 27 for killer of Indian River County deputy
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. Reaves is scheduled to be executed Oct. 27. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said he plans to attend the execution and wants to make sure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County deputy uniform. The execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025.

Marc Raczkoski, the victim's brother, said the signed warrant brings closure after 40 years of waiting. Marc Raczkoski was 22 years old when his 29-year-old brother was killed. He said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family, with his parents ending traditions like Christmas trees and holiday decorations. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." Marc recalled the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything, when a friend from the police department drove him to the hospital but kept him in the car too long, which made him realize his brother had not survived.

Deputy Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County on Feb. 23, 1986. He was shot four times and killed. Authorities arrested Reaves days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves, who was 37 at the time, was extradited to Indian River County and confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death. Marc said his brother was calling a cab for Reaves when he was killed. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me," Marc said.

Flowers said the coming execution will bring healing to the agency. Marc Raczkoski described his brother as someone always focused on public service who was quick to make people laugh and enjoyed fishing and the outdoors. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said her group has concerns about the pace of executions and the transparency of the selection process. "We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why," Hanna said. Deputy Raczkoski is buried at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce.
hero.article_text: At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." cards.headline: Vero Beach man faces felony charge for illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
cards.teaser: A 20-year-old Vero Beach man was arrested early Monday after a traffic stop near Americana and 90th Avenue led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. Hughes faces a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge.

According to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier.

Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie MRI tech told sedated patient 'nobody can see what I do to you,' criminal complaint says
cards.body:
A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told the woman "Nobody can see what I can do to you" before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. Lucie police criminal complaint.

Gabriel Cruz, 42, faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. The patient told investigators she woke up during the assault and alleged Cruz was rubbing her hair afterward, then cleaned her mouth with a white towel, the complaint states.

Port St. Lucie police responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital shortly after 8 a.m. on Sept. 14 after the patient reported the assault. The patient had been admitted after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. She told police medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep when she was transported for an MRI at about 4 p.m. The patient, whose primary language is Spanish, described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt.

"In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said.

Hospital staff identified Cruz as a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there, but the video showed Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time.

"Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Niemczyk said.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital released a statement saying the facility contacted law enforcement and ended Cruz's assignment when the allegation was reported. The hospital said it has assisted law enforcement throughout the investigation and remains focused on supporting the patient.

"It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital," Niemczyk said.

Julie Stoyka, director of the Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee, said the impact of such assaults can bring feelings of shame, fear, confusion, guilt and anger. The program's rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

cards.headline: Card skimmer discovered on 7-Eleven gas pump in Fort Pierce prompts investigation
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation. Arlo Bess said he routinely checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps and discovered the device after pulling on the card reader.

"So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training." After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added.

Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed."

Card skimmers are devices that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. He noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers.

Santiago and Bess warned that card skimmers can also be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said.

To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said.

Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for false bomb threat, fourth targeting school in week
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday on a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat through the FortifyFL school safety reporting system because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore, faces a charge of making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

The threat was submitted around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present at the school. The message stated someone was walking by the boys bathroom and heard people saying there were bombs in the school that would blow up during third period. Sheriff John Budensiek said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating.

Surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. Another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students, but he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. Taylor told deputies he made the threat because he was tired of being in class and wanted to get out of third period. Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce.

The arrest marks the fourth bomb threat connected to Martin County High School in just over a week and a half. Budensiek said investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. The initial threat came through Russia, and the last two remain under investigation. Principal Lori Vogel said in a statement that false threats cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. Budensiek warned that what students think is funny can have long-term consequences, including difficulty getting a job in the future. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation.

cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup. Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the local effort across 28 locations.

The nonprofit, volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful. County volunteers participated at Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris.

Linda Emerson participated at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island. She said picking up pieces of plastic allows people to realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
hero.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

Rehki Jyquan Hughes was stopped near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 when a deputy noticed his black Dodge sedan had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window.

Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier. Deputies said they saw marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

cards.headline: 15-year-old arrested after false bomb threat at Martin County High School
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student confessed to sending a hoax bomb threat that disrupted the school Tuesday, authorities said. The arrest comes amid multiple recent school threats in the area.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after confessing to sending a false bomb threat to the school, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office and school district.

Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. School resource officers and Criminal Investigations Division detectives traced the message back to Taylor, who confessed to sending the threat during the investigation, according to the Sheriff's Office.

The threat was reported through FortifyFL, Principal Lori Vogel told families. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The Sheriff's Office immediately began investigating and identified the apparent source of the message. The district notified families Tuesday that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent.

The arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks, according to the Sheriff's Office. Investigators said they can only link Taylor to this specific threat.

School officials said students found to have been involved in making threats could face both school disciplinary action and legal consequences. The district reminded families that FortifyFL is an important tool for reporting legitimate safety concerns, but knowingly submitting false information or making a false threat can have serious consequences.

False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Vogel said. She added that they can cause fear, disrupt learning, and place a burden on students, families, school employees, and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said threats made anonymously, through text messages, online, or through other electronic communications, can still be traced and investigated.

cards.headline: Brother of slain Indian River deputy reacts to Oct. 27 execution date for killer
cards.teaser: Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant for William Reaves, who murdered his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986.
cards.body:
Marc Raczkoski said he finally has closure after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing his brother, Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski, in 1986. The execution is set for Oct. 27.

"It gives closure," Marc Raczkoski said at his brother's grave at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce. "It's finally over."

Richard Raczkoski was 29 years old when he was shot four times and killed on Nov. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Authorities arrested William Reaves, then 37, days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death.

Marc Raczkoski, who was 22 at the time of his brother's death, said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate," he said. He described standing beside his brother's grave for 40 years, waiting and wondering. "Feels like everybody forgot," he said.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the execution will bring healing to the agency. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers said. The sheriff said he plans to attend the execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," Flowers said.

Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said her organization has raised concerns about the rapid pace of executions and the transparency of the selection process.

Marc Raczkoski said his brother was always focused on public service and liked to fish and enjoy the outdoors. "He was quick to make you laugh," Marc Raczkoski said. "For what he did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there."

This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." Sheriff Eric Flowers said he plans to attend the execution and that the coming date has lifted weight off the agency after nearly 40 years.

Marc Raczkoski, the slain deputy's younger brother, said the warrant brings closure after decades of waiting. "It's finally over," Marc Raczkoski said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened.'" Reaves was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

He described his brother as someone always focused on public service who was quick to make people laugh and liked to fish and spend time outdoors. Sheriff Flowers said he plans to attend the execution because he wants to make sure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025.

cards.headline: Indian River County deputy and K9 Penny rescue missing dementia patient in Gadsden County
cards.teaser: Deputy Sam Lewis and his K9 partner Penny helped locate and pull to safety an 84-year-old woman with dementia who had been missing for 30 hours in Gadsden County while attending a certification course.
cards.body:
An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his K9 partner helped rescue a missing 84-year-old woman with dementia in Gadsden County near Tallahassee while attending a K9 certification course. Deputy Sam Lewis and K9 Penny joined bloodhound search teams from across the state to locate Margaret Myles Ellis, who was reported missing on Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before.

Ellis had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area to assist in the search. Ellis was found approximately 30 hours later in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety.

The Indian River County K9 unit includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. Lt. Margaret said Penny and other dogs participated in a rotated search effort. Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned home and resumed their duties.

Sheriff Jaworski expressed pride in the deputy and the entire K9 unit. He also highlighted the unique role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies, noting that dogs provide a way for officers to connect and express things they see and hear every day. Ellis was reunited with her family after the rescue.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man faces felony bump-stock charge after traffic stop near Americana and 90th Avenue
cards.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock after a traffic stop near Americana and 90th Avenue turned up what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

Rehki Jyquan Hughes was stopped shortly after midnight Sept. 21 when a deputy noticed his black Dodge sedan had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier.

Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. He was also charged with misdemeanor marijuana possession. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

hero.headline: MRI technician told sedated patient 'Nobody can see what I do to you' before alleged assault at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital
hero.body:
A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital in Port St. Lucie allegedly told her "Nobody can see what I can do to you" before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a criminal complaint obtained by police.

Gabriel Cruz, 42, faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. Police characterized the patient as vulnerable and sedated during the alleged Sept. 14 assault.

"In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie police chief. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital."

According to the criminal complaint, officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital shortly after 8 a.m. on Sept. 14 after a patient reported being sexually assaulted by a technician. The patient told investigators Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head.

The patient said she was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. Medication made her drowsy and she drifted in and out of sleep, the report states. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt.

The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room.

Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time.

"Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Niemczyk said.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: "We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual's assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient."

cards.headline: Man charged after being shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police determined a man armed with two knives was the primary aggressor in a parking lot confrontation that led to him being shot in self-defense outside a restaurant. Christopher Harris now faces felony charges.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police determined a man armed with two knives was the primary aggressor in a parking lot confrontation that led to him being shot in self-defense outside a restaurant, and Christopher Harris now faces felony charges.

Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard for reports of a shooting and found Harris suffering from a single gunshot wound to his chest. Police say Harris was armed with a knife and shot after starting an argument with another man over a parking space.

The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police recovered and secured a firearm. Investigators say Davis shot Harris in self-defense.

Police said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said.

When Davis left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911.

During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment.

Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. Police said Harris was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sunday after he was treated and released from the hospital.

cards.headline: Card skimmer found on Fort Pierce 7-Eleven gas pump prompts police investigation
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are investigating after a card skimmer was discovered Monday morning on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue. Officials are urging residents to check tamper seals and use tap-to-pay to avoid card fraud.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are investigating after a card skimmer was discovered Monday morning on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, found the device while checking the card reader before pumping gas.

"So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training." Bess locked his truck and informed the store manager, who said she had never seen one before.

A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. No other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but Bess filed a police report.

Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed," Santiago said.

Santiago and Bess warned that card skimmers can also be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said.

To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers.

If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud and attempting to extract information from credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said.

hero.headline: Martin County High School sophomore arrested after bomb threat; told peer tip couldn't be traced
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School sophomore was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after allegedly texting a bomb threat and telling another student the tip could not be traced back to him. Noah Taylor now faces charges of making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb.

The threat was reported through the FortifyFL portal around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present at the school. Investigators traced the report to a student identification number associated with Taylor. When questioned, Taylor acknowledged making the report but initially claimed it came from other students, according to the affidavit. He could not provide identifying information about the alleged students or describe their voices, and he refused a request to search a personally owned Chromebook.

Investigators reviewed school surveillance footage and saw Taylor walking past a bathroom with another student. That student told investigators Taylor said a tip would be created anonymously and would not be traced back to Taylor, according to the affidavit. Taylor was then advised of constitutional rights and agreed to speak with investigators. His laptop was confiscated as evidence. The investigation resulted in probable cause to book the student for false report concerning planting a bomb.

Taylor was taken into custody and transported to the Martin County Sheriff's Office jail before being transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said Taylor can only be linked to this specific threat.

Principal Lori Vogel said false threats are neither harmless nor funny. She added that false threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms or other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday. Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the local effort as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup. Keep Martin Beautiful served as the local coordinator for the event.

County volunteers participated at 28 locations, including Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

Keep Martin Beautiful is a nonprofit, volunteer-based community action organization founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful. The organization said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris.

Linda Emerson participated in the cleanup at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island. Emerson said by picking up pieces of plastic, volunteers can realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

hero.headline: Death warrant signed for killer of Indian River County deputy, execution set for Oct. 27
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Oct. 27, marking the culmination of a 40-year wait for the victim's family and the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Raczkoski, 29, was shot four times and killed on Nov. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Days later, authorities arrested Reaves, then 37, in Albany, Georgia. Reaves confessed to the killing, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. He was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death.

The death warrant brought relief to Marc Raczkoski, the deputy's younger brother, who was 22 when his brother was killed. Standing at his brother's grave at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce, Marc said the news brought closure after decades of waiting. For nearly 40 years, when people asked what happened to his brother's killer, Marc had to tell them nothing had been resolved. The wait took a toll on his entire family. His parents stopped decorating for Christmas and holidays were never the same.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the execution will bring healing to the agency. Flowers, who has pushed for the death warrant to be signed, plans to attend the execution. He said he wants to make sure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County deputy uniform. If carried out, the execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025. Reaves has one last chance at an appeal. Marc Raczkoski described his brother as someone always focused on public service who was quick to make people laugh and liked to fish and spend time outdoors.

"Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." cards.headline: 15-year-old arrested for false bomb threat at Martin County High School
cards.teaser: A Martin County High School sophomore was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after investigators traced a hoax bomb threat back to the student.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old student was arrested Tuesday after threatening Martin County High School, according to the district. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office said school resource officers and Criminal Investigations Division detectives traced the message back to Taylor. During the investigation, Taylor confessed to sending the threat, according to the Sheriff's Office. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district.

The threat was reported through FortifyFL, Principal Lori Vogel previously told families. The Sheriff's Office immediately began investigating and identified the apparent source of the message. The district notified families Tuesday that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent.

The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said they can only link Taylor to this specific threat. School officials said students found to have been involved in making threats could face both school disciplinary action and legal consequences. The district also reminded families that FortifyFL is an important tool for reporting legitimate safety concerns, but knowingly submitting false information or making a false threat can have serious consequences. False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Vogel said, adding that they can cause fear, disrupt learning, and place a burden on students, families, school employees, and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said threats made anonymously, through text messages, online, or through other electronic communications, can still be traced and investigated.

cards.headline: Vero Beach traffic stop yields illegal Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana
cards.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man after a routine traffic stop near Americana and 90th Avenue led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. Rehki Jyquan Hughes faces a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge.

A deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier.

Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
cards.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested Rehki Jyquan Hughes, 20, of Vero Beach early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

A deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier.

Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward. Deputies also found multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council approves $2.2 billion mobility plan with $1.7 billion funding gap
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading Monday of a $2.2 billion mobility plan that aims to address traffic congestion through 2050, but the city faces a $1.7 billion funding shortfall. The plan updates mobility fee schedules for the next four years and outlines infrastructure projects including new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. Final approval from City Council is required before the updated plan takes effect on Dec. 31.

The mobility fees are applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners. Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge at the Monday council meeting. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020.

A city official told the council that the plan identifies infrastructure needs through 2050 based on current analysis, but cannot solve all funding problems. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan," the official said. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one tool to help fund future projects and create the funding necessary to build infrastructure.

Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. "Mobility fees may need to supplement that," Samples said. The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid-, and long-term projects. Resident Laura Milsom said the growth is impossible to ignore on local roads and supports requiring developers to help pay for traffic management. "The population increased so rapidly," Milsom said. "A lot of traffic backups."

hero.headline: Martin County High School sophomore arrested after bomb threat traced to student ID
hero.body:
A 15-year-old sophomore at Martin County High School was arrested Tuesday on a second-degree felony charge after investigators traced a bomb threat reported through the FortifyFL portal to his student identification number and confiscated laptop. Noah Taylor was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb.

The threat was reported on the FortifyFL portal around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present. Investigators traced the report to a student identification number associated with Taylor. When questioned, Taylor acknowledged making the report but initially claimed the report came from other students. According to the affidavit, Taylor could not provide identifying information about the alleged students or describe their voices. The student also refused a request to search a personally owned Chromebook.

Investigators reviewed school surveillance footage and saw Taylor walking past a bathroom with another student. That student told investigators Taylor said a tip would be created anonymously and would not be traced back to Taylor, according to the affidavit. Taylor was advised of constitutional rights and agreed to speak with investigators. Taylor's laptop was then confiscated as evidence.

Taylor was taken into custody and transported to the Martin County Sheriff's Office jail before being transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. The original threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The Sheriff's Office said the arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks. Investigators said Taylor can only be linked to this specific threat.

Principal Lori Vogel said false threats are neither harmless nor funny, adding that false threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms or other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

cards.headline: More than 1,000 volunteers clean 28 Martin County sites in International Coastal Cleanup
cards.teaser: Volunteers turned out at beaches and parks across Martin County on Saturday, collecting plastic and debris to protect marine life and birds.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.

Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the effort at 28 locations, including Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park. The nonprofit volunteer organization has served as the local coordinator for the international event since its founding in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful.

Volunteers removed plastic and debris that threatens wildlife in coastal areas.

"We are also able to help protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these innocent creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris," Keep Martin Beautiful said.

Linda Emerson participated at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island.

"By picking up these pieces of plastic, we can realize how much we are using in our own lives and choose to make a difference," Emerson said.

hero.headline: Execution date set for Oct. 27 for killer of Indian River County deputy
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Oct. 27 and would mark Florida's 18th this year. Reaves has one last chance at an appeal.

Marc Raczkoski, the slain deputy's younger brother, said the warrant brings closure after nearly 40 years of waiting. He was 22 years old when his 29-year-old brother was buried at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce. Marc said for decades when people asked what happened to his brother's killer, he had to answer that the execution still had not happened.

Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot four times and killed on Feb. 23, 1986, after answering a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Authorities arrested Reaves days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves, who was 37 at the time, confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death.

Marc Raczkoski said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family. His parents stopped decorating for holidays and never put up another Christmas tree. He recalled the middle-of-the-night knock on the door when one of his brother's friends from the Fort Pierce police department took him to the hospital, and he knew from how long they talked to him that his brother did not make it.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the coming execution lifts weight off the agency and will be a moment of healing. Flowers said he plans to attend the execution because he wants to make sure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform.

The execution follows 19 executions in Florida in 2025, which set a modern-day record. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said the group has raised concerns about the rapid pace and transparency of the process, including how people are chosen for execution and the impact on corrections staff. Hanna said her own family member was murdered and that she understands everyone processes grief differently, but that another death did not give her family closure or peace.

Marc Raczkoski described his brother as someone always focused on public service who was quick to make people laugh. He said the pain will always be there, but the coming execution finally brings closure for what Reaves did to Richard.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
cards.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

A deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window.

Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire, according to the report. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.
